Tiong Bahru's quieter streets tell a story of changing shops, tastes and crowds after hipster heyday
article:
On weekends, Tiong Bahru stirs to life early. Brunch-goers head to cafes like Plain Vanilla , Hello Arigato and Matchaya, while early risers have already picked up their bakes from Tiong Bahru Bakery by mid-morning.

Across the road, the market is busier. Residents and visitors jostle for groceries in the wet market downstairs before heading up for chwee kueh and fried prawn mee, joining queues that can stretch well past the next stall.

All around are the walk-up flats that have long defined Singapore’s oldest public housing estate. Built by the Singapore Improvement Trust in the 1930s, the low-rise blocks have rounded corners and curved balconies, with spiral staircases winding up their backs, in a streamlined Art Deco style rarely seen in public housing since.

The buzz beyond these familiar haunts has softened since Tiong Bahru's heyday as a hipster enclave in the 2010s.

Several independent cafes, bookstores and restaurants that once helped put the neighbourhood on Singapore's lifestyle map have since closed or moved elsewhere.

"The crowds have thinned. Anyone walking Eng Hoon Street on a Saturday can see it," says Bryan Goh, Singapore country manager of sleep and bedding brand Heveya, which has occupied a three-storey conservation shophouse in the estate since 2016.

Despite the quieter streets and departure of some longstanding names, new businesses are still opening in Tiong Bahru, introducing fresh dining and retail concepts.

Healthcare, fitness, beauty and wellness operators have also joined the tenant mix, while established businesses are refreshing their premises.

Property analysts point to a combination of rising operating costs, changing consumer habits, a shrinking residential catchment and greater competition from other lifestyle precincts as possible reasons for the decline in footfall.

Even so, Tiong Bahru's unique heritage and residential character continue to appeal to businesses seeking a foothold in the neighbourhood.

A flourishing enclave and the pressures that followed

Tiong Bahru was built in the 1930s mainly as a residential estate. Its transformation into a lifestyle destination took off in the early 2010s, when independent cafes, boutiques and bookstores started moving in.

“Footfall was limited then, but these businesses could drive their own traffic because people would travel for what they offered,” Ethan Hsu, founder and CEO of retail-focused real estate advisory firm Catbird, tells EdgeProp Singapore .

Relatively low rents allowed businesses to experiment with distinctive, independent concepts that made Tiong Bahru special, adds Hsu, who grew up around the neighbourhood.

As it became more popular, investors bought commercial units to ride the demand from retailers and F&B operators, and rents went up.

“One tenant said back in 2013 that his rent had quadrupled in six years. Those costs were passed on to customers, which weakened demand,” says Hsu.

“Ironically, the enclave’s success in the 2010s led to its decline.”

Real estate consultancy Cushman & Wakefield’s (C&W) analysis of URA Realis data provides some indication of how rents have risen over the past decade.

Average quarterly median ground-floor retail rents in Tiong Bahru’s core heritage and lifestyle precinct increased from $4.62 psf per month in 2016–2019 to $7.02 psf per month in 2023–2026.

These figures — based on properties along Yong Siak Street , Eng Hoon Street, Seng Poh Road, Eng Watt Street and Tiong Poh Road — are indicative given the limited number of transactions and their irregular frequency, C&W notes.

As commercial units in Tiong Bahru are privately held by numerous different owners, there is little visibility into precise rents and occupancy rates.

Catbird’s Hsu notes: “What we can say is that across the wider market, rents are still creeping up while occupied space shrinks. So it is not a collapse of the market, but a symptom of market churn.”

Meanwhile, the Covid-19 pandemic also took a toll on businesses, accelerating changes in consumer habits as more people turned to e-commerce and food delivery.

With lower footfall and higher costs putting a strain on operators, some cafes and shops shuttered or relocated.

Among them were some of the very establishments that had helped make Tiong Bahru the place to be.

Stalwarts depart as newcomers enter the mix

Property investor Peter Chiu has witnessed the turnover of businesses in the estate firsthand.

He bought an apartment in one of the conserved blocks in 2020, rented it out to residential tenants, and has since sold it.

“When I first bought the apartment, Prive Cafe occupied one of the ground-floor units. By the time I sold the apartment, the cafe was gone, and now it’s a new restaurant, Magpie,” Chiu says.

He has seen businesses come and go, including an influx of new dining concepts catering to younger crowds.

“Even a corner bak kut teh shop has become a Toast Box,” Chiu says. “But like most neighbourhoods in rejuvenation, it will go through this period of pain first.”

Several familiar names have left the estate over the years, including Forty Hands, Open Door Policy, PS.Cafe Petit and independent bookstores BooksActually and Woods in the Books.

Hsu observes that the tenant mix now includes more lifestyle services — the likes of healthcare clinics, fitness studios, beauty and wellness operators, art galleries and showrooms.

Some F&B players are also going smaller, with more takeaway counters and grab-and-go formats, and fewer sit-down cafes.

Tiong Bahru's predominantly residential setting presents another challenge for businesses.

With shops and homes sitting close together, many operators must navigate residents' concerns about noise and other disturbances, which can limit activities such as alfresco dining and late-night operations.

“The 2010s were the anomaly, not the baseline,” Hsu says, describing Tiong Bahru's boom at the time as part of a cycle fuelled by novelty, social media and a pioneering group of trendy concepts.

“That cycle has run its course, the same way it did in Holland Village , Chip Bee Gardens and Ann Siang Hill with Club Street.”

Fewer residents and growing competition

Tiong Bahru's retail scene may also be feeling the effects of a shrinking pool of residents living in and around the estate.

Fewer residents in the neighbourhood:

C&W research points to a steady decline during the past decade. The resident population within the Tiong Bahru and Tiong Bahru Station subzones fell about 9%, from about 29,200 in 2016 to 26,400 this year.

The number of residents per dwelling unit also decreased from 2.6 to 2.2 over the same period in those subzones.

“A smaller residential catchment may have moderated growth in neighbourhood-based retail demand,” says Wong Xian Yang, head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia at C&W.

“While Tiong Bahru has historically drawn visitors from beyond its immediate catchment, a declining resident base may nevertheless have reduced routine and repeat visitation that supports day-to-day retail spending.”

At the same time, visitors have more locations to choose from than a decade ago. These include newer lifestyle clusters such as New Bahru, Joo Chiat and Keong Saik.

Visitor traffic is therefore likely to be distributed across a broader range of precincts today, Wong adds.

A resident identified only as Ng, who has lived in a Tiong Bahru shophouse for about 2.5 years, has noticed the quieter atmosphere, though it is a change he personally welcomes.

He believes some visitors have turned their attention to other up-and-coming lifestyle destinations. “I think people are drawn to the novelty of places like New Bahru,” Ng says.

While New Bahru, located just a short distance away, has probably diverted footfall from Tiong Bahru, Catbird’s Hsu highlights a key difference in how the two precincts operate.

With a concentrated, curated mix of more than 60 brands under one roof and a clear identity, New Bahru has one owner deciding its tenant mix, programming and marketing as a single destination.

“That’s exactly what Tiong Bahru’s fragmented ownership makes so difficult,” Hsu says. “Its trade mix, by comparison, has become diluted, with no critical mass or strong draw to pull people in.”

Fresh experiences in a historic neighbourhood

Amid the changing retail landscape, some businesses continue to find new opportunities in the neighbourhood and build on the heritage, architecture and residential character.

Established businesses are upgrading their premises, while newer arrivals are adding to the estate's dining and retail offerings.

Heveya, for instance, chose to renovate its existing flagship on Eng Hoon Street instead of relocating.

The homegrown bedding retailer’s revamped showroom, unveiled in late October after about three months of renovation, offers a more immersive experience for customers.

“Refreshing the space within the same heritage shophouse felt like a natural next chapter for us, allowing us to build on our roots while showcasing our brand’s evolution over the years,” says Goh.

Heveya’s clientele mainly comprises environmentally conscious buyers in their 40s to 50s who are willing to invest in premium organic sleep products, though Goh has noticed more shoppers in their 30s to 40s keen to experience the showroom.

Where the showroom once existed mainly to let customers try mattresses and learn about natural latex, it now showcases the materials, craftsmanship and philosophy behind the brand alongside the beds.

At the heart of the 2,200 sq ft space is a striking handwoven ramie installation by Bali-based Argentinian artist Clelia. Around it, woven fibre panels, wooden-bead wall art, natural blinds and sculptural bamboo lighting bring texture to the shophouse's heritage architecture.

Curved banquettes and low lounge furniture invite customers to linger, while a tactile display traces latex from tree to mattress.

During EdgeProp Singapore 's visit, the team pointed out the calming earthy palette of what they call “mochaccino walls”.

Customers are encouraged to have a free spinal alignment check before trying the beds. Some come in simply to sleep on the mattresses, occasionally for hours, before deciding on a purchase.

Given the nature of its products, Heveya relies on customers making planned visits rather than passing footfall. “Nobody buys a mattress on impulse between coffees. People come to us deliberately, and many of them live a few doors away,” Goh says.

The showroom also serves a purpose beyond immediate sales, as it helps Heveya build “brand awareness, customer relationships and long-term brand equity”, he adds.

Goh sees value in operating from a heritage shophouse, which he believes offers an experience that conventional retail spaces cannot replicate. “The architectural character and sense of history create a more intimate relationship between the space and its surroundings,” he says.

After nearly a decade in Tiong Bahru, he also considers the estate’s slower pace a good fit for Heveya: “A quiet estate suits a brand built around rest.”

Crafts and curiosities among market stalls

Outside the shophouses, smaller players are finding their way into the estate through humbler, less conventional spaces.

Sideway, a craft and design stall run by photographer-turned-potter Keneth Tan and co-founder Yasha Lai, occupies just 93 sq ft on the first floor of Tiong Bahru Market, among sundry shops lining its outer edge.

Both founders hold weekday jobs and open Sideway mainly on weekends. The market stall offers a smaller-scale setup that suits their part-time operation, without committing to a large retail unit.

For Tan, though, opening in a market was always the intention, as the pair wanted craft to be accessible to everyone.

“As makers ourselves, we believe that craft should exist beyond galleries and exhibition spaces, and instead be more present in everyday life,” he says.

Sideway's shelves hold an ever-changing mix of zines, local ceramics and secondhand objects, including pieces picked up during trips to Japan.

Being in a market also influences their selection, as Tan and Lai lean towards functional pieces such as tableware that people can easily use at home.

Many customers find the stall through social media, which skews the crowd younger, though its location in Tiong Bahru Market also draws people of different ages. Those who stop by include seasoned collectors and people encountering handmade crafts for the first time.

Tan speaks fondly of their neighbouring stallholders, who have been welcoming. Early on, while changing a light bulb, the pair accidentally tripped the main circuit-breaker. The owner of a nearby hardware stall helped them contact the market management to sort it out.

Since then, they have come to recognise familiar faces among their regulars, alongside curious passers-by who wander in to browse or chat.

“That’s the spirit we hope to bring to the neighbourhood: a space where people can slow down amid the hustle and bustle of the market, and perhaps even the fast pace of life in Singapore as a whole,” Tan says.

Bookstore set to move in as bakery gets a makeover

A familiar name in Singapore’s literary circles is preparing to make Tiong Bahru its new home — Book Bar, the homegrown bookstore and cafe founded by Alex Chua and Sara Ng.

Having opened in a Duxton Road shophouse in July 2023, the bookstore will soon relocate to a 2,172 sq ft space at Tiong Bahru Community Centre, roughly twice the size of its existing premises. Renovations are expected to be completed by December.

Chua has spoken about plans to host more book launches, readings and community activities at the larger venue, according to local media reports. Plans include cooking and flower-arrangement workshops, food pop-ups and a wider selection of books.

Book Bar’s arrival in Tiong Bahru bucks a trend. Two other bookstores, once fixtures of Yong Siak Street, have exited in recent years.

Elsewhere in the estate, Tiong Bahru Bakery (TBB), a neighbourhood stalwart since 2012, has given its original outlet on Eng Hoon Street a makeover.

The 60-seat flagship reopened in September 2025 following its first major refurbishment. The redesign includes a self-service island where customers can select their own pastries.

A refreshed visual identity by Singapore branding agency Foreign Policy Design Group features whimsical illustrations and a crescent-shaped logo whose lettering takes a modern spin on the estate's 1930s Streamline Moderne architecture.

“Taking inspiration from Tiong Bahru's architecture gives that identity a connection to where we started, rather than introducing something that could belong anywhere,” says a TBB spokesperson.

“We want returning customers to recognise the bakery they love, while still finding something fresh to enjoy.”

More reasons to linger after dark

Best known for its cafes and bakeries, Tiong Bahru is also gaining a livelier evening crowd at its restaurants.

Magpie debuted on Eng Hoon Street in early 2025, serving what its founders call borderless soul food.

The restaurant is a venture by New Zealand chef-owner Eliot Thomas and Kurt Wagner, founder of Kafe Utu on Jiak Chuan Road and Tamba on Duxton Road.

Magpie’s menu changes regularly, and some ingredients are sourced from Tiong Bahru Market right across the road.

“Tiong Bahru built its name on mornings: bakeries, kopi and brunch. What's changing is that people now want a reason to stay into the evening, and the estate suits that,” says Thomas. “It’s walkable, it has character, and it doesn’t feel like a mall.”

On Tiong Bahru being quieter than before, Thomas admits he never saw it at its busiest, having been in Singapore for only two years.

“I know Tiong Bahru as it is today, and that is the version I chose to open in,” he says.

Dinner trade has been steady, while lunches from Friday to Sunday have also performed well. About half of Magpie's diners live in or near Tiong Bahru, with the rest travelling from across the island.

Families typically dine early in the evening, and groups gather later in the week.

A recently launched cocktail programme gives people a reason to drop by after work or after dinner elsewhere. Taco Tuesdays and skewer nights keep regulars coming back, and collaborations with neighbouring businesses are in the works.

Thomas is also mindful of keeping neighbours onside, given the residential surroundings.

Magpie keeps tables available for residents who walk in, and is careful about noise, deliveries and waste management.

“The aim is for Magpie to feel like it belongs to the estate rather than just being located in it,” he says.

“I’d rather add a steady stream of diners who respect the place than a noisy crowd that wears out the goodwill.”

----------

What could give Tiong Bahru's retail scene a boost?

A precinct-wide, structured placemaking strategy could help reinvigorate Tiong Bahru and attract more visitors, says Wong Xian Yang, head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia at Cushman & Wakefield.

He suggests an approach similar to the Place Plan developed for the Kampong Gelam historic area.

“Beyond individual events, such an approach would provide a coordinated framework to strengthen Tiong Bahru's identity, curate tenant mix, activate public spaces, and create recurring experiences that encourage visitation,” Wong says.

Ethan Hsu, founder and CEO of Catbird, points out that there remains a catchment, however small, as people still live and work around the estate.

Although Tiong Bahru lacks scale — it does not have enough shops and restaurants to reach the critical mass that pulls crowds to Katong or Kampong Gelam — Hsu thinks that can become an advantage with a clear, well-executed plan to curate the right experiences.

More collaboration among merchants could help put such a plan into action. Businesses may coordinate opening hours, share marketing costs and work out sensible alfresco dining rules with residents.

One approach is to meet the needs of residents and workers nearby, with everyday services, a good neighbourhood cafe and convenience shopping so that they spend locally every day.

Hsu also suggests bringing in destination footfall with concepts that cannot be found anywhere else. Examples are small chef-led restaurants, specialist shops, maker studios running workshops, and galleries open in the evenings.

However, he reckons these ideas will likely only work if rents are affordable and can encourage experimentation.

“Right now, rents do not reward creativity and innovation. Costs are too high, and failure is too expensive, so operators play it safe or do not open at all,” Hsu says.

Daytime activities, including weekend markets and the odd car-free morning, could also encourage visits while minimising late-night noise and disruption to residents.

Tiong Bahru could make more of its heritage story too. “This was Singapore’s first planned housing estate, and walking trails or a small museum in a restored pre-war flat are things that are not easily replicable,” Hsu adds.

Any efforts to increase visitor traffic would have to take into account the estate's predominantly residential setting.

Bryan Goh, Heveya's Singapore country manager, and Eliot Thomas, Magpie's chef-owner, both emphasise that businesses and activities should be mindful of residents and respect their needs.

“In Tiong Bahru, where families live directly above shops, it has to be considerate: daytime, small-scale, and something residents want to join,” Goh says. The kampung spirit, as he puts it, “is built by neighbours who keep showing up for one another”.

For Hsu, the goal is not necessarily to replicate the buzz and crowds of Tiong Bahru's former heyday.

“We are not going to get 2012 back, and we should not try,” he says.

title: WeWork appoints Ryan Jans as Asia Pacific president
article:
WeWork has appointed Ryan Jans as regional president for Asia Pacific (Apac), overseeing its operations across eight countries including Singapore, the flexible workspace provider said in a Nov 20 release. He is based in Sydney.

His priorities include strengthening the performance of WeWork’s existing portfolio, deepening relationships with members and landlords, and delivering a consistent workplace experience across its markets.

“WeWork is in an incredibly strong position in Apac, and there is so much more ground to cover,” Jans said.

Jans previously led WeWork’s revenue teams across Asia Pacific and Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA).

WeWork has 58 locations in Apac, part of a global network of about 600.

WeWork said demand drivers differ across the region. In Singapore, global technology companies, including Chinese businesses setting up regional operations, are driving demand for flexible workspace.

In South Korea, demand is more locally driven, with Korean technology businesses playing an important role.

In Australia, where WeWork marks its tenth anniversary this year, the company sees opportunities in improving occupancy and growing enterprise demand, particularly in Sydney.

John Santora, CEO of WeWork, said Jans’ knowledge of the region and commercial expertise make him well placed to build on the company’s momentum.

title: Hong Leong Holdings completes over $40 mil office tower revamp and digital integration of business operations
article:
Hong Leong Holdings , the private property arm of Hong Leong Group Singapore, completed the renewal of Hong Leong Building , its 45-storey CBD office tower, in September.

At 158m, the building was among Singapore's tallest when it opened in 1976. The asset enhancement programme, which began in October 2023, includes upgrades to the podium frontage, common areas, and lift lobbies. A new sheltered alighting area at Level 5 replaces the former drop-off point along Telegraph Street.

The asset enhancement and the digitalisation of the developer's operations involved a total investment of over $40 million. "The renewal of Hong Leong Building and our digital transformation are complementary investments that strengthen both our physical assets and business capabilities," says Quek Kon Hui, executive director of Hong Leong Holdings.

The new integrated platform connects the developer's sales, leasing and finance functions, and was developed with advisor PwC Singapore and technology partners Showsuite, SAP and Planon Asia. The system has been used at its recent residential launches, including Lentor Hills Residences , Lentor Central Residences , Penrith and Tengah Garden Residences . Hong Leong Holdings says it has improved data visibility and accuracy by 30%, and operational efficiency by up to 65%.

Showsuite has supported the launches and sales of six Hong Leong Holdings projects since 2020, starting with Penrose . "This new level of partnership now covers the downstream progress payment workflows, API integration with their SAP account and several new customised features," says Showsuite CEO Karamjit Singh.

The new features include a bank reconciliation function for incoming digital payments. According to Singh, they prepare Hong Leong Holdings for changes such as digital signing for property transactions and a move to cheque-less payments. "The eight-month exercise effectively removes layers of disjointed systems and streamlines their workflow," he adds.

title: First Fila 'sport-fashion hotel' opens in Shanghai; Andaz debuts in Australia with Gold Coast property
article:
Hyatt Asia Pacific has broadened its Asia Pacific portfolio with two new properties in Shanghai, China and Gold Coast Australia.

In China,  Fila House Shanghai — the world’s first Fila-branded ‘sport-fashion hotel’ — opened on Nov 13, Hyatt said in a Nov 24 release.

The hotel is located in Shanghai Anta Center,  the global innovation hub and corporate campus for Chinese sportswear giant Anta Group. The group holds the rights to operate the Fila brand in China, Hong Kong and Macao.

The property is part of Hyatt’s JdV portfolio, comprising a global collection of independent boutique hotels.

Fila House Shanghai has 108 rooms and suites. The suites feature design themes based on the sportswear brand’s golf, tennis and athletic lines.

The biggest suite at the hotel, the 196 sq m (2,110 sq ft) Biella Presidential Suite, is designed around Fila’s signature red, navy and white palette, while also celebrating the brand’s Italian heritage. It includes a private terrace overlooking cityscape and park views.

Amenities at Fila House Shanghai include the Pure Wellness & Activity Space on the third floor. It features a fitness club, an activity pool, and indoor swimming pool, alongside group training spaces, yoga and Pilates studios, changing and shower facilities, and relaxation and recovery areas.

The hotel has two restaurants: 1911 Ristorante and Privato. The former, named after the year Fila was founded, is an all-day restaurant offering Italian and Mediterranean cuisine through an à la carte buffet concept.

The latter offers Fujian and Cantonese cuisine, with a focus on seasoned ingredients and thoughtful presentation.

In Australia, Andaz Gold Coast opened on Nov 16. It marks the country’s first Andaz property.

The 202-room hotel is located in Broadbeach within The Star Gold Coast integrated resorts and entertainment precinct. It was designed by Australian architecture firm DBI Architects, with interiors by design studio Hachem.

The hotel features four dining destinations, with a highlight being Nove Restaurant and Bar, which features fire-led Mediterranean cooking and interiors designed by MAS Architecture Studio.

Another highlight is the hotel’s signature experiences, which include poolside Pilate and breathwork sessions, barbecue evenings on selected Thursdays, and a daily Golden Hour, which offers in-house guests complimentary beverages and snacks in the evening.

title: More than number crunchers: How quantity surveyors are gearing up for the future of building
article:
Suppose you inherit an old landed house and decide to undertake a major renovation to turn it into your family home.

You engage an architect, settle on the design and agree to a contractor’s quotation of $400,000. However, the contractual terms are loosely defined, with no firm completion date.

The renovation progresses more slowly than expected. Halfway through the works, the contractor unexpectedly revises the cost to $600,000.

Where will you find the additional $200,000? What assurance is there that the renovation will be completed on time without further cost overruns?

This is a scenario that Colin Kin, president of the quantity surveying division of the Singapore Institute of Surveyors and Valuers (SISV), says happens all too often and illustrates the importance of cost planning and contract management.

Had a quantity surveyor been involved from the outset, the homeowner would have received a detailed breakdown of the estimated costs, from windows and doors to floor finishes and bathroom fittings.

The quantity surveyor could also have worked with the architect to keep the design within budget while helping the owner negotiate clear terms with the contractor — such as payment schedules, changes to the works, completion deadlines and penalties for delays.

"Most people are already familiar with what architects, engineers and contractors do," says Kin, who is also managing director of Rider Levett Bucknall (RLB) in Singapore.

"But there's this unseen profession that nobody ever considers if you're outside of the built-environment sector. Somebody needs to take care of the costs and the contracts."

Natalie Yong, first vice-president of SISV's quantity surveying division, also recognises the financial and emotional significance of building or renovating a home, where families may spend many years of their lives.

"If you're going to live there, you want to feel good about your home. You don't want to think, 'Wow, it cost me so much. I overpaid for this,'" says Yong, managing director of LCH Quantity Surveying.

What quantity surveyors do, and what's next

Quantity surveyors keep building projects on time, on target and on budget throughout the lifecycle — from the design stage to tendering and construction.

They are often described as part lawyer, part accountant and part project adviser, though the value they bring is not always well understood.

Their clients can range from homeowners undertaking extensive renovations or rebuilds to property developers building condos and hotels.

Quantity surveyors also work on public-sector and infrastructure projects such as HDB developments, hospitals, MRT stations, roads and airports. On the construction side, contractors may engage these professionals to prepare tender bids, manage costs and handle payment claims.

Limited awareness of quantity surveying as a career has made attracting new talent a challenge, while the profession also faces difficulties retaining experienced practitioners.

In February, the Building and Construction Authority set up a dedicated QS Workgroup to examine these issues and future-proof the profession.

In September, the workgroup came up with recommendations to attract, develop and retain quantity surveyors, and help firms operate more efficiently and profitably.

"As projects become larger and more complex, the future of quantity surveying must be about greater value and taking on more strategic roles in project delivery," said Second Minister for Finance and National Development Indranee Rajah when announcing the workgroup's recommendations.

'Count every dollar, make every dollar count'

Long before construction workers arrive on site, quantity surveyors are already working out what a building will cost and whether it is financially viable.

They calculate the cost of essentially every aspect of a building — from structural elements and façades to interior finishes.

These calculations then form the basis of cost estimates, feasibility studies and pre-tender estimates, which help clients set realistic budgets, and guide architects and engineers in designing within those limits.

They also evaluate contractors' bids and prepare contracts that set out costs, timelines and responsibilities.

Once construction kicks off, they monitor expenditure, assess the cost of changes and verify payments for work done.

"A quantity surveyor also looks at value engineering, finding ways to cut waste in a building, whether in productivity or sustainability," notes Eugene Seah, second vice-president of SISV's quantity surveying division and CEO of DLS Consultancy.

The aim is to achieve the best value for money, which does not always mean choosing the cheapest option.

"Count every dollar and make every dollar count," as Kin puts it.

Developers typically set their construction budgets with target profit margins in mind, based on the expected selling prices of their units.

That means quantity surveyors must work closely with other consultants to stick to the budget.

"If we go over that fixed budget target, the developer is not going to make money because their selling prices can't be increased much," Kin says.

The bigger picture in creating value

Besides keeping construction costs in check, quantity surveyors also assess how much a building will cost to operate and maintain over time.

They often take into account the durability of materials and equipment, energy consumption, disposal and replacement costs.

This process, known as life-cycle costing, helps determine whether spending more now could be more economical in the long run.

Kin cites the example of a hotel owner who wants to install thick, luxurious carpets expected to last 15 years. However, given the heavy foot traffic in a hotel, the carpets may need replacing after just five years.

"Maybe you don't need to spend so much money on a thick carpet. You can choose a cheaper, medium-grade one that can be replaced more regularly to keep it looking fresh," he suggests.

"We look at which option is the most efficient from a cost-to-use perspective. It's not about just choosing the cheapest one but which will give the biggest bang for buck," Kin adds.

Quantity surveyors can also use their knowledge of construction methods, technology, materials and design to identify alternative solutions that reduce costs, speed up construction and improve overall project outcomes.

Seah recalls a building that was initially designed with three basement levels to house a certain number of carpark lots.

Drawing on his experience with other developments, he suggested incorporating the parking spaces into the ramp linking the basement levels: "Why can't the ramp be the car park itself?"

This improved the car park's space efficiency, reducing the average floor area required per parking lot by about 15.6%.

He notes that the client saved $8 million by building two basements instead of three, while still having the same number of carpark lots. The project was also completed more quickly.

"Quantity surveyors can add a lot of value once they understand design and technology, and bring all these together instead of having people working in silos. It's not just fixated on cost," Seah says.

A stronger voice at the table

Identifying ways to improve a project is one thing, but having the confidence and communication skills to convey those ideas effectively is another.

Yong observes that quantity surveyors tend to be “the quietest people” during meetings with clients and other consultants. "Many don't speak up," she adds.

She believes this needs to change — quantity surveyors have to become more vocal, navigate difficult conversations and take on a greater advisory role.

This comes as AI is taking over more of the profession’s routine work, such as calculating quantities and analysing cost data.

"The quantity surveyor has to exercise professional judgement. Our experience in handling many kinds of projects enables us to have a more nuanced view on how to proceed," Yong says.

"AI can give you data and point out discrepancies, but it can't decide for you and tell you how to diagnose it. You need to apply judgement and advise the client," she continues.

Agreeing that having a human in the loop will remain important, Seah sees the profession taking on a bigger role in bringing together architects, engineers, contractors and other stakeholders.

This requires quantity surveyors to interpret information, express themselves clearly and help clients understand the implications of each decision, Seah highlights.

Kin describes quantity surveyors as increasingly becoming "skilled negotiators, communicators, integrators and peacemakers" who can empathise with different stakeholders, anticipate potential disputes and find solutions.

He adds that quantity surveyors are also equipped to manage uncertainty, from changing requirements to unforeseen costs and risks.

"Dealing with flexibility and unknowns, contingency management — that’s not something you can give to AI," Kin notes.

Getting on students' radar

Despite hundreds of entry-level vacancies available in quantity surveying, many students are unfamiliar with it as a career option.

There were about 320 such vacancies in March 2026, according to Ministry of Manpower data cited in the QS Workgroup report.

However, Singapore has no dedicated degree or diploma programme on quantity surveying.

The National University of Singapore (NUS) recently introduced a new specialisation in Contract Management and Cost Engineering, within its Bachelor of Engineering (Infrastructure and Project Management) undergraduate programme.

Another pathway is the existing Bachelor of Building and Project Management programme at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, which offers training relevant to quantity surveying.

SISV has also stepped up its outreach efforts, including organising a competition with the NUS Department of Built Environment earlier this year. More than 60 students from polytechnics, junior colleges and International Baccalaureate explored cost, contracts and sustainability at the three-day challenge.

Yong hopes such initiatives will raise awareness of the career path and attract more students with a diverse range of interests and strengths.

"Every time I interview a candidate and ask why they studied quantity surveying, 90% of the time they answer, 'My maths is very good,'" she says.

While mathematical aptitude is essential, the profession also draws on a broad set of skills, including communication, negotiation and collaboration.

Yong also believes existing quantity surveyors can do more to encourage others to join the industry, by sharing what they find fulfilling about their work.

At the same time, part of the challenge in attracting talent may lie in the name "quantity surveyor" itself.

The QS Workgroup has recommended reviewing the title to better reflect the profession’s broad and strategic role.

"How to rebrand ourselves such that the youth will find it appealing is the biggest challenge we have at the moment," says Kin. "If we say 'quantity surveyor', nobody knows what we do."

Ideas floated during brainstorming have included "commercial manager" and "cost and contracts professional", although no new name has been decided.

Retaining talent and supporting firms

While a rebrand could help attract new entrants, retaining talent also requires better remuneration, manageable workloads and clearer career progression.

The workgroup has suggested improving the financial sustainability of firms so they can invest more in staff development and technology.

Kin points out that quantity surveying firms are often paid a fee agreed on at the start of a project, even when delays and changes lead to substantial additional work later that they may not be paid for.

"We’re burning hours and burning resources, which affects profitability," Kin says.

"If you had said it'll be $1 million on day one but it ends up costing you $2 million, there's no way you can increase salaries or give bonuses that year."

To tackle this, SISV is developing a Value Articulation Framework — a comprehensive list of core and value-added services — that will help clients and quantity surveying firms better define the scope and complexity of services from the outset.

The aim is to make things more transparent and give firms a clearer basis for pricing their services and charging for additional work, Kin says.

Celebrating those behind the scenes

Recognising the achievements of quantity surveyors could help build professional pride, raise the prestige of the profession and inspire the next generation to join the industry.

The QS Workgroup recommends both public- and private-sector clients to recognise firms’ exemplary contributions, be it at annual dinners, on digital platforms or through other channels.

Yong has often seen architects, engineers, landscape designers and other consultants recognised for their contributions at industry awards ceremonies, whereas quantity surveyors receive little to no mention.

"The [built environment] sector gives awards for the best architecture, engineering excellence for the most optimal columns and beams, and for landscaping of beautiful parks. But there’s nothing about quantity surveying," she remarks wryly.

She hopes such recognition will give younger professionals something to aspire to and help them feel valued for their contributions.

SISV is planning an awards ceremony for next year and has approached public agencies about recognising the profession's contributions.

Pride in the work and optimism for the future

Kin believes quantity surveyors have much to take pride in, especially the integrity, prudence and impartiality required when managing large sums of money.

"We deal with billions of dollars and ensure everything is above board and spent well, as stewards of value and stewards of public funds," he notes.

"When hospitals, HDB flats and MRT stations are built, we make sure taxpayers' hard-earned money is properly allocated. There is tremendous pride in that," Kin adds.

Meanwhile, Seah likens the profession's evolution to a metamorphosis, with a "blue ocean" of opportunities.

Having started his career using manual cut-and-shuffle methods and stencils, he is excited about the possibilities that digital technology and AI could open up.

"The next jump is going to be fantastic. But are we ready for it? That’s the question," Seah says, stressing the need to prepare both current and future generations of quantity surveyors for the shift.

For all the changes ahead, the three share an enduring enthusiasm for construction.

For Kin, part of the fascination comes from watching buildings take form from the ground up.

"When you go to a blank site, there's nothing there. Then they dig a hole, and they put in the piles, and you see this creation coming out of the ground,” he says.

"There's something magical about construction."

----------

Early sparks of a career in quantity surveying

Growing up, Eugene Seah found joy in assembling model aeroplanes and building things with Lego.

A third-generation quantity surveyor, he credits his grandfather — Seah Mong Hee, Asia’s first chartered quantity surveyor — and father, Seah Choo Meng, with nurturing his love for construction.

The young Seah began visiting construction sites at the age of eight and found satisfaction in watching buildings rise from the ground.

"I wanted to do something that makes a difference, where I can create value," says Seah, second vice-president of the quantity surveying (QS) division at the Singapore Institute of Surveyors and Valuers (SISV).

Even the most outstanding designs cannot be realised if the costs are prohibitive. "If it's too expensive and doesn’t make bankable sense, you can’t build it anyway," Seah adds.

Meanwhile, Natalie Yong, first vice-president of the QS division, had originally hoped to become an architect, but pursued quantity surveying when she was not accepted into architecture school.

With parents in the construction business, she had a headstart in the sector, traipsing to her first site at 14.

"I realised the underlying question was always, 'How much?' when my family was selling their products," she shares.

During her polytechnic years, Yong had an unusual weekend hobby: visiting condo showflats.

"I would study showflats and pore over their marketing materials, in and out. Seeing how things are being built also excites me," she adds.

As for Kin, his passion for construction began with a childhood storybook depicting a builder putting up a house from scratch, from laying the foundation and brick walls to installing the roof.

A knack for numbers later led him to discover that quantity surveying married two of his favourite subjects: construction and accounting.

"I just fell in love with my university course," says Kin, who was eager to start working after graduation. At SISV, he is now chairman of the central management committee and president of the QS division.

title: Million-dollar HDB flat deals may total up to 2,800 in 2027: Huttons
article:
Million-dollar HDB flat transactions are expected to reach between 2,400 and 2,800 in 2027, up from an estimated 2,100 this year, even as the wider resale market stays soft. The projections come from Huttons Data Analytics, the research and data division of Singapore real estate agency Huttons Asia.

The 2026 estimate is 31.7% higher than the 1,594 deals in 2025. Based on Huttons’ forecast, million-dollar flats made up about 8% of resale transactions this year, up from 6.1% the year before. Total HDB resale volume is estimated at 26,000 for 2026, similar to last year.

A wave of flats completing their five-year minimum occupation period (MOP) contributed to the rise in transactions of $1 million and above. More than 13,000 units fulfilled their MOP in 2026 — almost 70% higher than previous years — with about 60% located in mature estates such as Bedok, Queenstown and Toa Payoh.

The average price of million-dollar transaction stands at $1.16 million in 2026, based on HDB data downloaded as of Nov 19. The figure is 1% higher than $1.14 million in 2025.

By location, Toa Payoh, Queenstown and Bukit Merah recorded the most million-dollar deals in 2026.

Buyers are also favouring newer flats. Those aged four to six years made up 25% of million-dollar deals, five percentage points higher than in 2025.

Huttons said the newer, popular Build-To-Order projects that recently achieved their MOP include several developments in the Bidadari neighborhood in Toa Payoh, such as Alkaff Vista and Alkaff CourtView ; Bedok South Horizon in Bedok; and St George’s Towers in Kallang/Whampoa.

Other favoured projects were Northshore Straitsview in Punggol and SkyParc @ Dawson in Queenstown, where a five-room flat was sold for a record $1.818 million in October.

As these projects pre-date the Prime, Plus and Standard categorisations for HDB flats that were introduced in October 2024, they have fewer resale restrictions, Huttons noted. Prime and Plus flats have a 10-year MOP period, and are also subject to subsidy clawbacks upon resale.

Another 18,939 flats will meet their MOP requirement in 2027, with about 60% located in non-mature estates, a reversal from 2026. The top three towns with the highest number of flats fulfilling the five-year MOP are Yishun, Tampines and Punggol.

The strong pipeline of resale flat supply could thus continue to support million-dollar deals, according to Huttons.

For the wider HDB resale market, the firm forecasts prices to slip by 0.5% for 2026, in contrast to the 2.9% increase last year. This will mark the first decline since 2019.

Next year, overall HDB resale prices could bottom out and thus edge up by 0% to 2%, on an estimated 24,000 to 27,000 transactions, Huttons said.

title: Singtel vs StarHub: Which Telco Dividend Looks Safer Now?
article:
Singapore’s telcos
are fighting hard for your mobile plan.
That fight is showing up in their profits, but not in the same way.
If you’re choosing between the two for income today, the dividend from
Singapore Telecommunications Ltd
(SGX: Z74), or Singtel, looks safer.
Its core payout moves with profit, and profit is growing.
For
StarHub Ltd
(SGX: CC3), its dividend rests on a promised minimum while its profit and cash flow shrink.
Singtel reports by half-year and StarHub by quarter, so watch the labels – only StarHub’s free cash flow is covered here.

What pays for Singtel’s dividend?
Singtel runs four business units: Optus in Australia, Singtel Singapore, NCS and Digital InfraCo.
For the first half of its financial year ending 31 March 2027 (1HFY2027), Singtel’s directors approved an interim dividend of S$0.09 per share, up 9.8% from S$0.082 a year ago.
That payout has two parts, and they are worth keeping apart.
The core dividend of S$0.071 (S$0.064 a year ago) equals 78% of underlying net profit, the same share as a year ago.
Underlying net profit rose 10.4% year on year (YoY) to S$1.49 billion, though at constant exchange rates, it would have grown 15.9%.
NCS and Digital InfraCo grew revenue by 10% and 22% respectively.
In other words, the core dividend grew 10.9% because profit grew.
That kind of increase can repeat.
Buybacks
help on a per-share basis too.
Singtel has bought back 216 million shares for S$974 million so far under its S$2 billion programme.
The remaining S$0.019 (S$0.018 a year ago) is a value realisation dividend, which sits outside that 78% core payout.
Count it, but don’t build your budget around it.
Where could Singtel’s dividend come under pressure?
Singtel is not immune to the price war.
In Singapore, mobile service revenue fell 1.6% amid intense price competition.
Singtel Singapore’s EBIT fell 4.5%.
A one-off item also lifted its profit this half.
A first-time S$153 million dividend from Gulf helped cut net finance expenses by 55%.
There is no guarantee that boost returns.
Spending is rising too.
Singtel plans an additional S$1.2 billion of capital expenditure this financial year, mainly for data centres and AI, with S$0.7 billion of it to be funded by external partners and customer advances.
On the flip side, management raised its full-year operating profit growth guidance to between mid and high single digits.
Can StarHub’s 6-cent dividend floor hold?
StarHub holds the second-largest mobile market share and the largest broadband share in Singapore.
For FY2026, StarHub has reiterated a full-year dividend of the higher of S$0.06 or at least 80% of net profit adjusted for one-off items, paid twice a year.
Here’s the thing: a floor is a promise, not a profit.
For the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), service revenue rose 2.9% YoY to S$396.1 million.
Profit went the other way.
Net profit attributable to shareholders fell to S$3.9 million from S$22.1 million, a drop of 82%.
EBITDA fell 26.3% to S$72.1 million on lower gross profit, higher operating expenses and lower other income.
Operating expenses rose 11.0%, mainly on higher staff costs.
These figures exclude Ensign.
Free cash flow
is the lifeblood of dividends, and StarHub’s fell 79% YoY to S$26.0 million.
Net debt to trailing 12-month EBITDA rose to 2.76 times from 2.00 times at the end of 2025.
Interest cover dropped to 7.1 times from 9.4 times.
Management expects FY2026 EBITDA to come in at 75% to 80% of FY2025’s level.
With a smaller earnings base, the S$0.06 floor leans more on the promise than on profit.
What could turn StarHub around?
The price war shows in its consumer numbers.
Mobile revenue fell 6.0% YoY to S$121.2 million, as average revenue per user slipped to S$19.20 from S$21.70.
Enterprise is the bright spot.
Enterprise revenue rose 18.4% YoY to S$172.5 million, with managed services up 27.7%.
StarHub is also on track for S$70 million of savings by 2028, though only about 15% has been achieved so far.
On 24 November 2026, StarHub and
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4) announced definitive agreements for an all-share merger combining StarHub and M1 (expected to complete by 1H2027, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals).
This move would reduce Singapore’s mobile network operators from four to three and could ease competitive pressure over time.
Get Smart: Sort a dividend by what pays for it
A dividend paid from growing profit can keep growing.
A dividend held up by a floor needs the business to recover before it can rise again.
So when a company’s profit falls, ask which part of the payout it still promises you, and what it will use to pay.
If the business has to recover first, the dividend is promising more than the business is delivering.

title: 3 SGX Blue-Chip REITs Growing Underlying DPU by Up to 11.7%

A bigger distribution feels like good news, but whether it stays that way depends on what funded the increase.
Some increases come from leases that lift rents each year, while others are driven by cheaper loans or a property sale that will not happen twice.
The first kind is more likely to repeat, while the second may fade.
Three SGX-listed
real estate investment trusts (REITs)
have just reported higher distributions per unit (DPU), at least on an underlying basis, and each got there differently.

Why is Keppel DC REIT’s DPU growth built into its contracts?
Keppel DC REIT
(SGX: AJBU) owns 27 data centres across 10 countries.
For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), its DPU rose 11.7% year on year (YoY) to S$0.08571.
Net property income (NPI) grew 13.1% YoY to S$316.8 million, with the REIT crediting positive rental reversions and escalations, as well as the acquisition of Tokyo Data Centre 3.
Escalations are written into contracts, while rental reversions of around 14% for 9M2026 show that tenants accepted higher rents when their leases were renewed.
The REIT sold Kelsterbach Data Centre and lost income from Cardiff Data Centre, while finance costs rose 28.1% YoY.
A larger unit base following the September 2026 private placement also diluted DPU, as the new units were issued before the new assets began contributing rental income.
On 1 October 2026, Keppel DC REIT completed its purchase of an 88.62% effective interest in Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5.
Both properties are fully occupied, with in-place rents more than 30% below market levels, and management expects the deal to add 2.0% to DPU.
A S$625 million private placement funded part of the purchase, with yen-denominated debt covering the rest.
Aggregate leverage stood at 36.2% as at 30 September 2026 and is expected to rise to 38.8% on a pro forma basis.
Can FCT’s steadier growth continue?
Frasers Centrepoint Trust
(SGX: J69U), or FCT, is Singapore’s largest suburban retail mall owner.
For FY2026, its DPU rose 2.0% YoY to S$0.1235, marking a new high.
The increase was modest, but NPI climbed 15.7% YoY to S$321.7 million, mainly due to a full-year contribution from Northpoint City South Wing.
FCT
also reported higher passing rents across most malls, with retail committed occupancy at 99.7% as at 30 September 2026 and rental reversions of 6.6% for FY2026.
Cheaper borrowing helped too, as FCT’s average cost of debt fell to 3.2% from 3.8% a year earlier.
That benefit, however, depends on interest rates rather than shopper demand.
The acquisition boost is unlikely to repeat, as South Wing is now part of the comparison base.
Distributions from joint ventures also fell 11.7% YoY after a one-off special dividend did not recur.
FCT sold White Sands on 30 September 2026, removing the mall’s income from its portfolio.
Part of the proceeds will be used to repay borrowings and reduce aggregate leverage from 38.7% to 36.8%.
Meanwhile, NEX’s first-phase upgrade is 98% pre-committed and remains on schedule for completion by December 2026.
Why does FLCT’s headline DPU tell the wrong story?
Frasers Logistics & Commercial Trust
(SGX: BUOU), or FLCT, owns 118 logistics, industrial and commercial properties.
For FY2026, total DPU slipped 0.8% YoY to S$0.059.
Strip out distributions from divestment gains, however, and the picture changes, with DPU before these gains rising 9.4% YoY to S$0.057.
Capital distributions from divestment gains fell 71.3%, while higher finance costs also weighed on total distributable income.
The underlying growth has a contracted core, with FLCT pointing to higher annual rental increments from its L&I segment.
L&I occupancy stood at 99.1% as at 30 September 2026.
Across the whole portfolio, leases signed during the year carried rental reversions of 10.4%, while passing rents remained about 9% below market levels.
Other contributors are less dependable, as FLCT benefited from higher average Australian dollar and euro exchange rates, which could reverse.
Finance costs rose 4.6%, while its commercial properties were valued 8.7% below their carrying value and aggregate leverage increased to 39.2%.
Get Smart: Sort the growth before you count it
Behind every
DPU increase
are several sources of growth, and they do not all carry the same weight.
Start with what the leases promise, such as escalations and annual increments.
Then look at what management has achieved through rental reversions and higher occupancy.
Treat cheaper debt and currency gains as bonuses that may not last, and keep one-off distributions on a separate line.
Before celebrating your next DPU increase, ask yourself one question: if interest rates and exchange rates stopped helping, how much of that increase would still be there?

title: Want Quarterly Income? 3 Temasek-Backed Stocks Paying You More

The dividend grows only if profit does.
Is profit growing? STE won’t say until full-year results.
The group reports half-yearly and gives only business updates in the first and third quarters, so its 9M update carries no profit or cash flow figures.
Revenue offers the best clue.
It rose 10% year on year (YoY) to S$10.0 billion in 9M2026, or 13% excluding LeeBoy, a business STE divested on 4 September 2025.
The risk sits inside the formula.
If full-year profit stalls, the policy adds nothing to the dividend.
Why did DBS pay more while its profit fell?
DBS
declared a S$0.66 ordinary dividend for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), 10% more than the S$0.60 a year earlier.
It also declared a S$0.15 capital return dividend, unchanged from a year ago.
Together, the S$0.81 sits 8% above last year’s S$0.75.
The quarter itself was weaker.
Net profit fell 4.8% YoY to S$2.81 billion after markets trading non-interest income dropped to S$17 million from S$419 million.
Net interest margin narrowed from 1.96% to 1.87% as Singapore interest rates fell.
So why pay more? The core bank kept growing.
Commercial book income, which excludes trading, rose 4%, while customer loans grew 9.5% to S$478.58 billion.
Nine-month net profit reached a record S$8.82 billion, up 2%.
Here’s the thing: the ordinary dividend grew 10% while nine-month profit grew 2%.
In other words, DBS appears to be paying out a larger share of what it earns.
Its update gives no payout ratio, so that gap is worth watching.
For 2027, management expects total income growth in the mid-single-digit range.
CEO Tan Su Shan also warned that the outlook has become more uncertain, citing elevated energy prices, tighter financial conditions and geopolitical risks.
Is MLT’s 0.1% DPU increase worth anything?
MLT owns 172 logistics properties in nine markets.
Its distribution per unit (DPU) for 2QFY2027 was S$0.01816, up just 0.1% from S$0.01815 a year ago.
MLT’s fiscal year ends in March, so 2QFY2027 covers the three months to 30 September 2026.
The properties did better than the payout.
Net property income (NPI) rose 1.0% to S$154.8 million, helped by the redeveloped Mapletree Joo Koon Logistics Hub, acquisition in India and organic growth, mainly in Singapore.
A stronger renminbi and Australian dollar also helped, and currency gains can reverse.
Where did the rest go?
Distributions to perpetual securities holders rose 33.6% after MLT issued S$400 million of new perpetual securities ahead of a planned November 2026 redemption.
Carrying both issues at once is a cost that should ease once the old one is redeemed.
Other offsets look stickier.
MLT lost income from divested properties.
Portfolio rental reversion improved to 2.1%, but China stayed negative at -1.7%.
China, again, is the drag.
Aggregate leverage of 37.5% also flatters the balance sheet.
On a pro forma basis, it would have been 40.4%.
Get Smart: Measure the raise against what pays for it
Before you celebrate a higher payout, set its growth beside the growth of the money behind it.
At STE, a published rule ties the dividend to profit growth.
At DBS, the ordinary dividend grew 10% against nine-month profit growth of 2%.
At MLT, NPI grew 1.0% while DPU grew 0.1%, and costs took the difference.

title: Dividend Yield vs. Dividend Payout Ratio: What’s the Difference?
article:
Having covered
dividend basics
and compared
REITs and blue chips
in our first two guides, we turn to two key metrics every investor should understand.
Most beginners assume that a stock offering a 7% dividend yield is a better investment than one with a 4% yield.
This is a common rookie mistake – focusing solely on dividend yield because it shows you how much income you can receive.
However, a high dividend yield doesn’t tell you everything you need to know about a stock.
Experienced investors look beyond dividend yield and also examine the dividend payout ratio.
What Is Dividend Yield and How Do You Calculate It?
Dividend yield measures how much a company pays shareholders in annual dividends relative to its current share price.
If a stock trades at S$5 and pays annual dividends of S$0.25 per share, its dividend yield is 5%.
Even when the payouts remain unchanged, the yield can change with share price fluctuations.
If the share price falls to S$4 and annual dividends stay at S$0.25 per share, the yield rises to 6.25%.
Hence, yield alone is not a foolproof indicator of a good investment.
Dividend yields from the past are not an assurance of future dividends.
Companies can also reduce or suspend dividends without warning.
What Is Dividend Payout Ratio and Why Does It Matter?
The dividend payout ratio is the percentage of a company’s earnings that it distributes to shareholders as dividends.
Investors can tell how much of a company’s profit is paid to the shareholders and how much remains undistributed.
A company that earns S$0.50 per share and pays out S$0.25 per share in dividends will have a dividend payout ratio of 50%.
Singapore’s largest bank,
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05), paid out about 64% of its FY2025 earnings as ordinary dividends, or about 80% once its capital return dividends are included.
A sustainable payout ratio is generally considered to sit between 40% and 70%.
Earnings not paid out to shareholders can fund business expansion, repay debt or support other corporate purposes.
A company that consistently pays out a high share of its earnings might have less flexibility to manage unexpected challenges or sustain dividends during trying times.
Singapore real estate investment trusts (S-REITs), however, must distribute at least 90% of their taxable income to qualify for tax transparency.
Hence, REIT investors should focus on distribution-related metrics and
cash flow
instead.
Dividend Yield vs. Dividend Payout Ratio: Key Differences
Dividend yield and dividend payout ratio measure different aspects of a company’s dividend performance.
Factor
Dividend Yield
Dividend Payout Ratio
What it measures
Dividend income relative to share price
Dividends relative to earnings
Formula
Annual DPS ÷ Share Price
DPS ÷ EPS
Main purpose
Estimates income yield
Helps assess payout sustainability
Affected by
Share price and dividend changes
Earnings and dividend changes
Key concern
High yield may reflect a falling share price
High payout may leave little earnings buffer
Dividend yield helps investors assess potential dividend returns, whereas the payout ratio provides insight into dividend sustainability.
Neither metric should be used in isolation; investors should always consider the company’s financial health, such as cash flow, earnings stability, and debt levels before making investment decisions.
Can a Stock Have a High Dividend Yield but an Unsustainable Payout Ratio?
The short answer is yes.
Consider this:

Compared with Company A’s 5%, Company B’s 7% dividend yield is higher.
However, Company B is paying out more than what it earns with a 140% dividend payout ratio.
This puts pressure on its financial resources and increases the risk of future dividend cuts.
For a real-world case of a high yield paired with a stretched payout, consider
ComfortDelGro Corporation Limited
(SGX: C52).
It paid S$0.085 per share in dividends for FY2025.
At its share price of S$1.25 on 16 November 2026, that works out to a dividend yield of 6.8%.
ComfortDelGro paid out 80% of its FY2025 profit as dividends.
However, it kept its 1H2026 interim dividend at S$0.0391 per share even as PATMI (profit after tax and minority interests) fell 19.7% year on year.
With net debt rising to S$1.03 billion as at 30 September 2026, from S$730.1 million at the end of 2025, ComfortDelGro has limited flexibility to increase its payout.
Management, however, expects net gearing of 26.1% to ease by year end, as it typically peaks in the third quarter.
How Should Beginners Use These Two Metrics?
It is not about choosing between dividend yield and payout ratio, but about using both metrics together to get a complete picture when researching dividends.
When evaluating a dividend-paying stock, consider three simple questions:
Is the dividend yield attractive relative to the risks?
Is the company earning enough to support its dividend payments?
Has the company maintained or increased its dividends over time?
If the answer to all three questions is yes, you might have identified a promising dividend stock.
If any answer is no, treat it as a warning sign of an unsustainable payout or a yield trap, which we will cover in the next article of this series.
Ultimately, dividend metrics are not a standalone reason to invest, but a starting point for deeper research.
Get Smart: Look Beyond the Yield
While dividend yield measures annual dividend income relative to the share price, the payout ratio shows how much of a company’s earnings are distributed to shareholders.
A high dividend yield is only attractive if it is financially sustainable.
Rather than treating these metrics as an either-or, investors should evaluate them together to assess a dividend stock’s true potential.

title: Indonesia said to set palm oil export fee at 0.5% of value
article:
(Nov 25): Indonesia’s new commodities export agency plans to collect a service fee from palm oil firms worth 0.5% of the value of their outbound shipments.

Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia, or DSI, will charge the fee based on the value of shipments declared in export notices, and will exclude freight and insurance, according to people familiar with the matter. Exporters will also pay a fixed charge of 2.5 million rupiah (US$136 or $176) for each contract, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is not yet public.

Details of the fee structure, which have not been previously reported, have been closely watched by the industry ahead of DSI becoming fully operational next year. The agency, run by the country’s fledgling sovereign wealth fund, will oversee exports of commodities including palm oil, coal and ferro-alloys, which together account for more than US$60 billion in annual trade.

DSI’s creation has sparked widespread uncertainty across Indonesia’s vast natural-resources industries since it was announced earlier this year. The government has said it is intended to curb under-invoicing, a process in which exporters declare shipments below their true value and shift profits offshore.

President Prabowo Subianto said in May that such “leaks” and other practices cost the nation as much as US$150 billion annually. Danantara officials have sought to reassure businesses the new system, which comes into effect in January, won’t disrupt exports. Indonesia is the world’s largest palm oil producer and exporter.

A DSI spokesperson said information regarding the fee could not be confirmed.

See also: Malaysia palm oil industry says CPO tax-waiver window has passed

“We suggest that this figure not be interpreted as a cost established by DSI until an official clarification is provided,” the spokesperson said.

The fee was discussed at a meeting on Wednesday, the people said. The details confirm the additional cost will be within the single-digit dollar-a-ton range previously indicated by DSI chief executive officer Luke Mahony. Speaking at the Indonesian Palm Oil Conference in Bali earlier this month, Mahony said the agency planned to levy a fee to cover the services it provides, with the exact amount due to be announced in December.

The new fee will come on top of existing taxes and levies on Indonesian palm oil exports, some of which fund the country’s biofuel and replanting programmes. Those charges fluctuate with a government reference price set each month and currently amount to more than US$200 a ton.

title: India offers US$1.2 bil to boost heavy equipment production
article:
(Nov 25): India will provide 110 billion rupees in incentives to manufacture heavy construction equipment including cranes, excavators and tunnel-boring machines, part of a push to cut reliance on imports from China.

The eight-year programme will run through the financial year ending March 2034 and is aimed at building local manufacturing for advanced construction and infrastructure equipment, Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw told reporters after a cabinet meeting on Wednesday (Nov 25).

The move comes after China restricted exports of some construction equipment, threatening to complicate India’s infrastructure push. The country is a major user of tunnel-boring machines, drilling machines and piling rigs needed to build metros, railways, highways and hydropower projects.

Beijing this year tightened export controls on some heavy machinery destined for India as it is among the world’s biggest producers. In 2024, shipments of tunnel-boring machines made in China by German tunnelling equipment maker Herrenknecht AG were also delayed during a period of tensions between the two countries.

The government will provide component manufacturers and original equipment manufacturers with financial incentives linked to increases in sales, according to a statement.

The programme could support companies seeking to manufacture the equipment locally, including state-owned BEML Ltd, which is exploring domestic production of tunnel-boring machines, Bloomberg reported earlier.
