title: Shoppers are using AI agents to save them from the ‘annoyance economy’
article:
(Nov 25): US$650 off a cable bill. US$265 in forgotten money. A deal on a used car.

Users of AI agents like Meta Platforms Inc’s Muse are putting the helper bots to work on the niggling, time-sucking annoyances that define modern consumer life – the overcharges, unwanted fees and refunds that normally take flocks of emails or hours on the phone to resolve.

All in, Eddie Gudewill lined up over US$3,000 in savings in two weeks by putting Meta Platforms Inc’s Muse to work. The 37-year-old said the AI agent cut about US$650 from his annual cable bill, saved roughly US$600 annually by switching to a cheaper phone plan and negotiated US$2,000 off a used Dodge Ram 1500.

“It made it a lot harder for the car broker than dealing with a normal Eddie,” said Gudewill in Victoria, British Columbia, who described talking with the salesperson on the phone while typing into Muse and getting instructions in real time. “I was way better equipped.”

Consumers and their bots may not have the upper hand for long, though. Companies like Amazon.com Inc and JPMorgan Chase & Co have shut access to bots or are building their own tools to counteract them, citing customer security risks, among other things. AI agents also threaten to erode profits built on consumer inertia: customers who stay with a company or service out of habit or to avoid the hassle of switching and negotiating.

See also: Anthropic breaks below US$83 IPO price in premarket trading

American families lose at least US$165 billion each year in wasted time and lost money dealing with issues like customer service holds, spam calls and surprise fees and surcharges, according to a February study from Groundwork Collaborative, a DC-based economic think tank.

The group calls it the “Annoyance Economy", and Neale Mahoney, a Stanford University professor who co-authored the study, says companies intentionally make it hard for customers to right small wrongs or cancel services they no longer want to pay for.

AI agents' potential for fighting back against the annoyance economy is driving adoption. Instinct, a startup that runs an invite-only assistant by text message, reached a multibillion-dollar valuation within months of its debut. More than 10 million people in the US and Canada had set up Muse in its first six weeks, Meta Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said on the company’s Oct 21 earnings call.

See also: Zoom seeks Asia Pacific growth with AI beyond meetings

Casey Robinson, a 30-year-old software engineer in Atlanta, said she uses Muse as a way to “catch money I would've just let go".

She paid extra for next-day delivery on a US$168 black top that took two weeks to arrive. She used Muse to get a US$16 refund for the shipping and another US$36 refund on a bouquet of flowers she purchased that did not arrive as advertised. She then tasked the agent with combing through her recurring bills and subscriptions and flagging any potential savings. It recommended downgrading a streaming service subscription that could save her US$9 a month and potentially save her on her internet bill based on her usage.

“I feel way more in control of my time,” Robinson said. “I just feel empowered to do more things or tackle more.”

About one-third of leading US e-commerce, airline, online travel agency, hotel and reservation websites have already blocked Muse, according to research by Jefferies Financial Group Inc.

"We've noticed a significant uptick in blocking/implementing barriers to agent-based interactions, with new restrictions appearing almost daily,” Jefferies analysts Brent Thill, Maximilian Joseph and Ria Naidu said.

Amazon said it asked Meta to remove it from Muse and then blocked the agent in late September. The company said it was not told in advance that Muse would access its store, that Muse does not identify itself and that it appears to capture and store customer credentials. Amazon said it expects all AI agents to operate openly and let businesses opt out.

Earlier this month, United Airlines Holdings Inc announced plans to block third-party artificial intelligence agents from booking flights and accessing customer accounts. US banks like Charles Schwab Corp and JPMorgan Chase & Co have also blocked AI agents from moving money for customers and demanding more guardrails.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan,” Chief Executive Officer Jamie Dimon said on the bank’s third-quarter earnings call on Oct 13. The bank is building its own tools to deal with agentic AI.

Investors are taking note. Shares of major banks, insurers and online travel agencies slid in September as Muse gained popularity after its Sept 8 release.

A Goldman Sachs basket of stocks exposed to consumer inertia has fallen 5% since Muse launched, compared with a 6.7% drop for the S&P 500. The basket tracks companies that rely on customers staying put out of habit or to avoid the hassle of switching services.

In a Sept 25 note, Barclays strategists Kannan Venkateshwar, Lauren Bonham and Ross Sandler described a world where consumers embed AI agents in different streaming services and instruct them to activate and cancel subscriptions based on the release of certain shows or sports seasons.

But the Barclays strategists argued that companies too can use AI technology to outsmart consumers. Businesses can deploy their own agents to create more customised prices or come up with personalised services to make customers less eager to switch.

“Businesses are likely to adapt their offerings to increase switching costs for consumers in more subtle ways by using their own versions of agentic tools,” Venkateshwar, Bonham and Sandler said.

Meta, for its part, leaned heavily on the agent’s ability to save consumers money. Soon after the debut, Alexandr Wang, the company’s chief AI officer, touted the idea that users could save up to US$1,000 with Muse on X. Under the “ideas” tab on the application itself, users could find inspiration in the “Financial Management” section for ways to use Muse to save money.

Among the prompts, Muse can “find and cancel those random subscriptions you forgot about", “help you get your provider to lower” your internet bill or “pick the best rewards card to use”.

Meta says shopping is the most common use for Muse but the agent also helps with money chores people put off. According to Meta, users have found unclaimed money, got a year of payments refunded on a subscription they forgot about, and found cheaper fares on trips they had already booked. Meta claims people choose which apps Muse connects to and can cut off access at any time. The company also claims passwords and logins are stored separately.

Some companies are leaning in. Meta says more than 40 partners, including OpenAI, Visa, Mastercard and Bank of America, are helping build a shared set of rules for how personal AI agents work with businesses. Meta also says Walmart now lets shoppers link their accounts to Muse and buy directly with the agent.

Anne DeSpain, 56, a consultant in Park City, Utah, saw a prompt on Muse offering to help her find lost money. The AI agent said it could search for unclaimed property that fit her name and past addresses, meaning money or assets that a company couldn’t deliver to its owner. So she plugged in the information. Muse came back with possible matches, including some that belonged to other people with similar names.

Then the agent stumbled. When DeSpain asked Muse to file the claims, it was able to open the web browser but could not fill out some of the information like her phone number, address and Social Security number. She also ran into glitches within Muse’s interface: A dropdown menu did not scroll far enough to complete the form. DeSpain finished the process on her computer outside of Muse.

DeSpain ultimately reclaimed around US$265, including money tied to a recovered toll account, a previous mortgage and a rebate through her car insurance. Still, she has reservations about giving Muse access to all her accounts and has so far only connected her email and calendar for optimisation.

“When you're using a personal agent, it's a bit of a black box; you don't really know what’s behind it,” DeSpain said.

People have to trust that agents working on their behalf are truly getting them the best deal, but that may grow murky if companies that develop the agents earn money through advertisement, referral fees or commissions, according to Justin Brookman, director of technology policy for Consumer Reports.

“Is the agent working on my behalf 100% or does the company have mixed interests?” Brookman said. “It is an issue of gamesmanship.”

For now, Gudewill thinks his bots are giving him an edge. But he doesn't expect that advantage to last forever.

“Price discrepancies get arbitraged away over time,” Gudewill, who writes an investing blog called the Goodwill Investing Journal, said. “And that'll probably happen here.”

title: IOIPG Malaysia REIT ends trading debut marginally below IPO price
article:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 25): IOIPG Malaysia Real Estate Investment Trust (KL:IOIREIT) ended its Main Market debut just marginally below its listing price and recouped most of its losses on Wednesday.

The trust opened at 87 sen versus its initial public offering (IPO) price of 91 sen per share, and fell to as low as 86.5 sen. IOIPG Malaysia closed at 90.5 sen, valuing the trust at a little under RM5 billion, as more than 36 million shares changed hands.

“We are not in a short-term business,” IOIPG Malaysia executive chairman Datuk Lee Yeow Seng said at a post-listing news conference. “We are here for the long run. What we want to try to achieve is to create value for our stakeholders, including our investors, our tenants, as well as our partners.”

The decline comes even after IOIPG Malaysia cut the final price by five sen in Malaysia’s largest-ever REIT IPO following lukewarm investor reception. A portion of the IPO was undersubscribed and had to be allocated to other categories of investors. Overall, demand from the average retail investors came in only slightly above the available shares.

The trust will also have to brave prospects of rising interest rates and other market uncertainties.

IOIPG Malaysia has an initial portfolio of nine properties valued at RM7.66 billion, anchored by IOI City Mall in Putrajaya, alongside six hotels operating under Marriott International’s brands and two office developments.

See also: IOI Properties defends Malaysian REIT IPO pricing as parent trades 40% below book, sees room for upside

The last REIT to be listed was Paradigm Real Estate Investment Trust (KL:PARADIGM), which opened flat in June 2025. Big Caring Group Bhd (KL:BCG), the most recent entrant to the Main Market, also opened below its IPO price in its trading debut.

On Wednesday, Kenanga Investment Bank initiated coverage on IOIPG Malaysia with ‘outperform’ call and target price of RM1.20, joining Affin Hwang Investment Bank that rated the trust a ‘buy’ with target price of RM1.12 ahead of the listing.

At its opening price of 87 sen, the implied distribution yield rises to 7.28% from 6.96% based on its IPO price. The trust has a distribution policy of paying at least 90% of its distributable income to unitholders on a quarterly basis.

See also: DayOne said to pause US IPO plans on data center, market concerns — Bloomberg

The spin-off listing forms part of the efforts by sponsor IOI Properties Group Bhd (KL:IOIPG) to pare down its borrowings and strengthen its balance sheet. The property developer also previously said it was exploring a separate trust for its Singapore assets.

The IPO raised about RM2 billion entirely for IOI Properties, with no fresh capital raised by the trust itself.

Maybank Investment Bank Bhd and AmInvestment Bank Bhd are the joint principal advisers, joint global coordinators, joint bookrunners, joint managing underwriters and joint underwriters for the IPO.

DBS Bank Ltd is a joint global coordinator and joint bookrunner.

CIMB Investment Bank Bhd, Hong Leong Investment Bank Bhd, RHB Investment Bank Bhd and UOB Kay Hian (M) Sdn Bhd are the joint bookrunners and joint underwriters. Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Ltd is also a joint bookrunner.

title: SK Hynix, Samsung to jolt won with US$33 bil year-end demand
article:
(Nov 25): South Korea’s artificial intelligence (AI) chip windfall is unleashing a wave of year-end currency flows, potentially pushing the won into its next phase of gains.

SK Hynix Inc and Samsung Electronics Co are poised to convert much of their massive export earnings to pay for US$33 billion ($42.6 billion) of third-quarter dividends, as well as record employee bonuses, in won. They will also need more of the local currency to cover large tax bills owed to the government from the AI hardware surge.

Those inflows are expected to help boost the won into the 1,200-per-dollar range by the end of the first half of 2027, according to Macro Hive and Korea Investment & Securities. Citing similar catalysts, Goldman Sachs Group Inc sees the currency strengthening to 1,280 next year, a roughly 5% gain from Wednesday’s level of 1,343.30.

Compressed into the next few weeks, these payouts bode well for the won, adding momentum to a 7% gain against the dollar so far this year. While overseas investors repatriating their dividends may create some won-selling pressure in the short term, record exports and a hefty current-account surplus also keep the currency’s 2027 upward trajectory intact, market watchers say.

“The bigger story is that exporters still have substantial dollar-selling needs,” said Vivek Rajpal, an Asian strategist at JB Drax Honore in Singapore. “The won’s appreciation trend has further to go despite weak sentiment towards AI stocks.”

See also: Aussie dollar set for worst month since 2013 on risk-averse selling

The won has rallied about 16% since hitting a 17-year low in June, as exporters led by chipmakers stepped up dollar sales to fund projects in South Korea. The currency is outperforming all its Asian peers this year and heading for its biggest annual gain since 2017.

South Korea’s two largest chipmakers are rolling out unprecedented dividend plans, driven by a memory-chip sales bonanza and a government push for local firms to boost shareholder returns.

Samsung is scheduled to distribute 30 trillion won (US$22.3 billion or $28.8 billion) in third-quarter cash dividends on Nov 27, which is about 12 times the average size of its quarterly payouts since the beginning of 2025, according to filings.

See also: Asia finds a surprise currency haven in AI-defying rupee

SK Hynix will pay its 14.1 trillion won dividend allocation for the quarter roughly by the end of the year, or more than 50 times the average size of its quarterly payouts since the beginning of 2025, company filings showed.

Samsung Electronics declined to comment. SK Hynix didn’t reply to a request for comments.

The payouts should support the won, said Moon Dawoon, an economist at Korea Investment & Securities. Companies are likely to convert more dollars into won to fund the payouts than what will ultimately flow back out as foreign investors repatriate their proceeds, she said.

To be sure, a large share of the cash will go to overseas shareholders, who tend to swiftly convert payouts back into greenbacks.

Foreign investors are estimated to receive about 15 trillion won from Samsung, while SK Hynix’s foreign investors are also slated to receive about half of its total payouts, according to Bloomberg calculations based on share ownership data.

In total, Samsung’s foreign investors will repatriate about half of the dividends they receive, amounting to about US$5 billion, as they’ve typically done in the past, estimated Lee Minhyeok, an economist at Kookmin Bank.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Those outflows could bite harder towards year end as global funds close their books and average trading volumes thin, a backdrop compounded by a stronger dollar and a pullback in semiconductor stocks, Lee said.

“There is considerable downside pressure” on the won this week ahead of the payouts, Lee said, referring to those from Samsung due Nov 27. “Some investors may convert their proceeds into dollars more quickly than usual to lock in their returns,” he added, while still expecting the won to rally in the longer-term period.

The chip boom is also set to deliver record worker bonuses early next year, potentially prompting chipmakers to sell more dollars to fund the won payouts.

Major chip, auto and shipbuilding companies will pay 60 trillion to 70 trillion won in bonuses in 2027, roughly six times this year’s 10.9 trillion won, according to Bank of Korea’s estimates.

Samsung and SK Hynix typically pay annual incentives in the first quarter, and the central bank estimated they alone will account for about 60 trillion won in the first three months of the year.

Bonus payments are likely to generate some temporary volatility in won trading, said Mingze Wu, a currency trader at StoneX Financial. “But overall the prevalent trend of the day will likely stay,” Wu added. Bonuses and special payments are “likely to be spaced out”.

Companies with December fiscal years must pay corporate taxes by the end of March, forcing exporters to raise won ahead of the deadline.

Thanks to a semiconductor-driven windfall, the South Korean government projects record corporate tax revenue of 478.6 trillion won for 2026, up 28% from last year. Tax payments will contribute about US$102 billion in net won demand and help lift the currency to 1,200 per dollar by mid-2027, Macro Hive estimates.

The chipmakers’ taxes and bonuses will be “a big deal”, JB Drax’s Rajpal said.

title: Aussie dollar set for worst month since 2013 on risk-averse selling
article:
(Nov 25): The Australian dollar is poised for its biggest monthly slide in more than 13 years as it extended losses on Wednesday (Nov 25), with the weakness in global stocks damping demand for currencies linked to growth.

The Aussie declined as much as 1.2% to 65.59 US cents, a level last hit on Dec 3. The latest slide widens its loss this month to 6.6%, which would be the steepest since May 2013.

It rose 0.4% earlier after inflation data exceeded economists estimates but the gain was quickly reversed as Asian stocks slid.

“Technically, the Australian dollar is looking oversold,” said Rodrigo Catril, senior foreign-exchange strategist at National Australia Bank Ltd. “But until we see an improvement in risk sentiment, the Australian dollar is likely to remain on the back foot.”

Losses in the Australian currency were exacerbated by some investors rebalancing their funds toward the end of the month and company sales against both the yen and US dollar, according to traders who asked not to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly.

See also: Asia finds a surprise currency haven in AI-defying rupee

The Aussie’s inability to sustain gains on the CPI data suggested that investors are acknowledging that the country’s pace of growth is slowing after a series of interest rate rises, which would keep pressure on its high-yielding currency.

“Further rate hikes may be harder for the RBA to deliver than they were at the beginning of the year,” said Michael Pfister, FX strategist at Commerzbank. Under such circumstances, the Aussie could struggle to benefit from data showing higher inflation, he added.

title: Malaysia's finance minister II said to mull role at Maybank
article:
(Nov 25): Finance Minister II Datuk Seri Amir Hamzah Azizan, a key architect of Malaysia’s fiscal reforms, is considering joining the country’s biggest bank, Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK), when his term as a senator ends next month, according to people familiar with the matter.

Amir Hamzah, who headed Malaysia’s largest pension, the Employees Provident Fund, before being appointed as finance minister II in a December 2023 Cabinet reshuffle, plans to leave the Cabinet when his term expires on Dec 11, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information.

“My focus is to do my day-to-day job,” Amir Hamzah said in an interview with Bloomberg Television’s Haslinda Amin on Wednesday. “Let’s finish the job.”

Maybank’s current chairman, Tan Sri Zamzamzairani Mohd Isa, has held the role since November 2020. Amir Hamzah’s appointment at Maybank isn’t expected to take place immediately after he leaves the government as it would require approval from the central bank, the people said.

“At this point of time, we are unable to comment on market speculation,” a Maybank spokesperson said.

See also: Malaysia’s EPF to boost overseas stakes, likes infrastructure

Under Amir Hamzah, Malaysia pressed ahead with efforts to repair its public finances, narrowing the fiscal deficit to an estimated 3.6% of gross domestic product this year from 5.5% in 2022. The government replaced broad subsidies for electricity, diesel and gasoline with more targeted assistance, generating about RM15.5 billion ($4.9 billion) in annual savings.

Those reforms provided a buffer when the Iran war sent oil prices surging this year, forcing the government to spend about RM40 billion to shield consumers from higher fuel costs while temporarily tightening eligibility for subsidised gasoline.

With more than 27 years of corporate experience, Amir Hamzah has described himself as a technocrat rather than a politician. Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim would respect Amir Hamzah’s decision not to extend his role as finance minister II, one of the people said. The central bank would have to approve Amir Hamzah’s appointment at Maybank, the people said.

See also: Malaysia tells data centres to cut off firms on US blacklist

Before joining the government, Amir Hamzah held senior roles across some of Malaysia’s biggest state-linked companies, including as the chief executive officer of shipping group MISC Bhd (KL:MISC), PETRONAS Dagangan Bhd (KL:PETDAG) and power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA). He also held leadership positions at state energy giant PETRONAS' lubricants business and companies tied to state investment funds Ekuinas and Khazanah Nasional Bhd.

He is the son of the late Tun Azizan Zainul Abidin, who served as the president and CEO of PETRONAS from 1988 to 1995.

“This is a very public role, and in the end, I am not a politician; I am a technocrat, and I know what I am good at and I know what I can contribute,” Amir Hamzah said in a 2024 interview with state news agency Bernama.

title: Private capital deals in Middle East have plunged by nearly 90%
article:
(Nov 25): The military conflict with Iran has led to a collapse in private-capital activity in the Middle East, according to the Global Private Capital Association.

Capital invested in the region plunged nearly 90% to US$2.4 billion over 113 deals in the first nine months of the year, compared with US$21.6 billion for 205 deals in all of 2025, according to the industry trade body.

A slower dealmaking environment has prevailed in the region while financial services and IT continue to dominate, according to Jeff Schlapinski, the GPCA’s managing director of research. Deals included Tabby Inc’s US$233 million funding round, backed by Arbor Ventures, Blue Pool Capital, HongShan Capital and Wellington Management Group. Global firms such as Temasek Holdings have, meanwhile, signalled long-term commitments to the region, announcing new office openings in the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

“While we do see an effect on deal activity this year, we also see many of these major global players are in it for the long term and committing to the region,” Schlapinski said on a call. “If you look out beyond the near term, the outlook and the fundamentals are still attractive to many investors.”

Looking ahead, private-credit investors say they see opportunities in funding diversification away from energy and investment in more resilient energy supply, the importance of which has only risen since the war. Brookfield held a first close of approximately US$2 billion in July for a new Middle East-focused fund anchored by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, accounting for the largest share of the US$2.8 billion raised in the region in the first nine months of 2026. The total was US$3.1 billion for all of 2025, GPCA data showed.

See also: German business outlook improves for seventh straight month

“My two cents is that what has happened regionally has done one thing among several — it will accelerate the transformation push of the GCC economies,” said Asad Hajiyev, senior executive officer and partner for the Middle East at Gemcorp, a London-based emerging markets-focused investment and private credit firm.

In December 2025, Brookfield Asset Management and Qai announced a US$20 billion AI-infrastructure joint venture in Qatar and selected international markets. In May 2026, Brookfield said its Middle East business was not affected by short-term volatility from the war.

See also: Australia to lower nominal economy estimate in budget update

In March 2026, Gaw Capital Partners launched the Gaw Tamkeen Nexus Fund, a GCC-focused growth equity vehicle that reached a first close of about US$150 million against a target of more than US$400 million and announced it is establishing a regional presence in Abu Dhabi and Riyadh.

Even as deals plummeted, a number of firms have expanded their presence in the region.

Ares Management received full authorisation for operations in Dubai in late September to arrange credit and advise on financing while EQT AB, Pantheon and Eurazeo have all opened offices in Abu Dhabi focused on private-asset secondaries and co-investment alongside sovereign wealth funds.

Investors are in a wait-and-see mood, avoiding radical decisions to either press ahead or exit, according to Alper Kilic, head of alternative credit at Ninety One in London.

“Our strategy is pretty much intact and we think that the growth opportunity across EM and in the region will remain robust,” he said.

title: Banks put data centre clients under microscope on AI chips — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 25): Banks from Citigroup Inc to Standard Chartered plc have launched sweeping reviews of data centre clients in the wake of tougher American rules to curb Chinese companies’ use of advanced US chips in Southeast Asian nations.

The banks join major Asian lenders — including Singapore’s DBS Group Holdings Ltd, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp and United Overseas Bank Ltd — in pushing for more disclosures from companies tied to data centres in Singapore, Malaysia and other countries in the region, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

The banks are pressing clients for further details on who uses their chips and seeking proof they’re in line with stricter export-control rules enacted by the US Commerce Department, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the queries are confidential. A key focus has been neocloud companies that stockpile chips and lease out computing power, with private equity firms, major players in financing Asia’s data centre boom, also receiving questions, the people said.

“We have reached out to our customers to understand the implications of the new rules,” Pauline Ho, OCBC’s group chief credit officer for wholesale banking, said in a statement. “Based on our engagement to date, we do not anticipate material concerns at this juncture, given that the vast majority of our data centre exposure is to US hyperscalers. We will continue to monitor developments closely.”

The industry sweep shows the key role that global banks will play in cracking down on diversions of US chips after the recent scandal involving Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang put the spotlight on the black market for US chips.

Standard Chartered, as well as banks operating in Singapore, are keeping the Monetary Authority of Singapore in the loop on their findings, the people said.

See also: Maybank reviews portfolio as chip curbs hit data centres

“MAS expects financial institutions to remain vigilant and assess the risks arising from their activities and exposures,” the Singapore financial regulator said in a statement.

Standard Chartered declined to comment. While the UK bank had been angling to increase its financing of Asian data centres and has been actively looking at graphics-processing unit deals for the past two years, it has been less aggressive than peers amid changing US regulations.

Wall Street has already been tightening lending standards as banks struggle to absorb a wave of artificial intelligence-related debt and cope with growing public opposition to US data centre projects. The new scrutiny raises the possibility that some older bank loans will be found in breach of covenants, forcing backers to wrestle with potential losses.

See also: Trump threatens to tax firms building data centres abroad

Loan exposure to data centres at DBS, OCBC and UOB accounts for a low-single-digit percentage of their total loan book as of the latest quarter, according to the lenders’ figures.

“Standard financing terms include warranties of compliance with applicable and prevailing domestic and international laws — any responsible bank would work with customers to understand how this is achieved,” DBS, Singapore’s largest lender, said in a statement. “DBS remains committed to supporting our data centre customers and continues to work on data centre financing transactions, subject to applicable regulatory requirements across jurisdictions.”

A UOB spokesperson said that the bank regularly reviews its financing portfolio and is engaging with clients on the new US rules. A representative for Citigroup declined to comment.

In Malaysia, the country that could have the most to lose in Southeast Asia from the latest US chip curbs, its biggest bank Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK) is reviewing its portfolio to assess how the restrictions could affect its data centre clients and their funding needs.

“There is an increased level of scrutiny that is obviously required, given the new developments and the new policies affecting the compute financing,” Michael Oh-Lau, chief executive officer of Maybank Investment Bank Bhd, said in an interview on Wednesday.

Nvidia, whose advanced chips and other products have helped power the AI boom, reinstated Huang as CEO this week, despite revelations of his affair with Alice Huang. Megaspeed International, her former company, is now on a US blacklist that bars it from buying advanced AI chips following allegations that it may have been smuggling Nvidia’s products into China.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The scandal brought attention to the networks linking Nvidia, Chinese customers and middlemen operating in overseas data centres. Nvidia is at the centre of multiple US probes over how China was able to harness its coveted chips. Some bankers now wonder, however, whether shifting political winds could eventually lead the US to ease chip-export restrictions on China.

For now they’re leaning into a bigger oversight role. The Commerce Department is requiring data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand to obtain licenses to buy advanced chips made in the US, closing a loophole that allowed the silicon to reach mainland China. In Singapore, a global financial hub that’s played a key role in financing data centres being built across Southeast Asia, the rules threaten to cool growth.

“We do not enforce America’s export controls, but we do not want Singapore to be used and abused as a conduit by companies to circumvent America’s export controls,” Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Tuesday. The city-state will facilitate US checks while taking “very firm enforcement actions” against companies that breach local law, he said.

Malaysia is ensuring compliance with the rules and is holding discussions with the US on the issue, according to the country’s Second Finance Minister Datuk Seri Amir Hamzah Azizan in an interview.

Banks in Southeast Asia, especially Singapore and Malaysia, are among the biggest funders of China-linked data centres and would take a hit should Chinese tenants leave, according to a Natixis report.

For deals in the works, US banks added new language to financing documents after the export controls were tightened. And lenders have frozen work on a US$480 million ($620 million) loan that would have funded Nvidia chips for use by China’s ByteDance, Bloomberg reported last week.

The scrutiny from banks is creating additional pressure for neoclouds. The new class of AI companies was already struggling with heavy debt loads and increasingly had to scrape together financial backstops from deep-pocketed tech firms to secure data centre capacity.

“You’re talking about placing limits on the ultimate use of the compute, which potentially makes certain projects less valuable and less resilient,” said Andrew Caridas, a partner at the law firm Ashurst Perkins Coie. “That’s going to be a concern.”

title: Asia finds a surprise currency haven in AI-defying rupee
article:
(Nov 25): The Indian rupee is Asia’s top-performing currency this month, joining a rally in the nation’s equities as investors double down on a hedge against the artificial-intelligence trade.

The currency rallied as much as 0.8% to 92.18 per dollar, its strongest level since March 12. It is also leading emerging-market currencies this quarter, a sharp turnaround after the central bank was forced to announce emergency support measures in early October.

Indian assets have rallied strongly this month even as most Asian stocks and currencies have floundered, as concerns over the AI trade spur a rotation into markets with less exposure to the theme. Overseas funds have poured nearly US$14 billion into local equities in November, after pulling unprecedented sums earlier this year, helping the rupee outperform most global peers.

Lower oil prices are adding to the tailwind by cutting India’s import bill and demand for dollars.

“The recent improvement in INR’s flow backdrop has scope to extend,” said Mitul Kotecha, strategist at Barclays plc. Lower oil prices are cutting India’s demand for dollars to pay for imports while strong foreign equity inflows are adding to the domestic supply of the US currency, he added.

See also: Singapore, China deepen yuan ties with focus on corporates

Barclays has a ‘tactical’ short position on the dollar/rupee, Kotecha said.

title: Russia oil loses price edge in India as Middle East exports rise
article:
(Nov 25): India’s imports of Russian crude are set to decline this month to pre-war levels as a revival of Middle East exports provides buyers with an abundance of cheaper supplies.

Sellers of Russian crude have been slow to cut offer levels to keep up with the falling prices of Persian Gulf oil, according to people familiar with the matter. Iraqi and Saudi Arabian grades have recently been priced at discounts to the Dubai benchmark while Russian Urals remains at a premium, they said, asking not to be named discussing commercial information.

Russia will still remain India’s biggest supplier but its grip on the market has weakened. Imports are poised to average about 1.7 million barrels a day this month, the lowest since February and nearly 40% below July’s record of 2.8 million barrels a day, according to Kpler. Higher freight rates are also eroding the competitiveness of Russian oil given the longer voyage to the subcontinent.

“Shipping from Russia, particularly from the Black Sea, remains expensive due to security risks and logistical uncertainties,” said Sumit Ritolia, senior manager of modelling at Kpler. “Indian refiners are increasingly looking at alternative supplies, not just to optimise crude costs but also to improve supply security and reduce dependence on any single source.”

Indian refiners had been trimming purchases before the Iran war as New Delhi and Washington negotiated a trade deal and the removal of US tariffs. But the conflict in the Middle East disrupted crude supplies to global customers and prompted India to prioritise its energy security.

See also: Europe is beating Asia in fight for gas supply disrupted by war

Overall, India’s crude imports this month are set to shrink to around 4.9 million barrels a day, according to Kpler, the lowest level since August. While Russian purchases are expected to decline, shipments from Iraq and Saudi Arabia are both set to hit the highest since February.

Indian imports of Russian crude are likely to remain near 1.5 million barrels a day in December and into 2027, continuing to rank among the country’s largest suppliers, Ritolia said. But a return to near-record levels seen earlier this year appears unlikely, he said.

title: Huawei found guilty of US criminal charges in landmark case
article:
(Nov 25): Huawei Technologies Co, China’s largest technology company, was found guilty of multiple US criminal charges, including money laundering, a conspiracy to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran and North Korea.

A federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, deliberated for about four days before reaching a verdict Tuesday in a rare US prosecution of a foreign corporation. The panel found the company guilty of 10 of 12 counts following an 11-week trial. Huawei was cleared of two conspiracy charges related to racketeering and obstruction of justice.

The verdict against one of China’s biggest and best-known tech giants lands at a delicate time for relations between the world’s largest economies, with the Trump administration tightening curbs on China’s ability to access American chips after revelations that Nvidia Corp’s Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence.

Even so, the years-old case is unlikely to affect the broader trade truce between leaders Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, who affirmed a commitment to keep ties stable in a summit last week. While that deal is set to expire in January, both sides have an incentive to prevent a deterioration that could lead to much higher tariffs and bans on essential items like rare earths, airplane parts and chip design software.

“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws,” said Brooklyn US Attorney Joseph Nocella. “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from US technology companies.”

Brian Heberlig, Huawei’s lead lawyer, focused on the company’s acquittal on two charges, including the so-called RICO racketeering count, which he called the government’s lead charge. The company said in a separate statement that the remaining charges have no merit and it will review its legal options.

See also: Indra raises revenue guidance to more than €12 bil by 2030

“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig said. The RICO charge “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge”.

When asked about the case, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said his nation “firmly opposes the US side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises”.

See also: Asia data centre sound out US clients to replace China demand

He added at the regular press briefing in Beijing on Wednesday that China backs the companies “in safeguarding their own legitimate rights and interests”.

The decision comes years after the Justice Department first filed charges against the world’s largest maker of telecommunications equipment. For most of that time, the company has been largely excluded from the American market under trade measures imposed by the Trump and Biden administrations in the name of national security.

The telecom titan has emerged as China’s de facto national chipmaking champion and is one of a handful of firms central to Beijing’s goal of dominating artificial intelligence and replacing American software and circuitry with local equivalents.

The case was publicly unveiled in early 2019 under the first Trump administration’s so-called China Initiative, a Justice Department programme to combat Chinese espionage and influence in the US. Prosecutors have since won numerous convictions against Chinese nationals, but have struggled in trials against large Chinese companies on American soil.

The jury of nine women and three men heard testimony from more than 60 witnesses during the 11-week trial. Huawei was convicted of a scheme to steal trade secrets from rival tech competitors during a 20-year period, including source code from Cisco Systems Inc, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile as well as proprietary information from Fujitsu Network Communications.

“Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion, and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies, they are serious crimes,” said James Barnacle, head of the FBI’s New York office. “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

In their verdict Tuesday, however, the panel rejected the government’s theory that Huawei had engaged in a racketeering scheme for more than two decades to “grow its global brand” into one of the biggest telecoms in the world.

The panel also rejected a US charge that Huawei obstructed a federal grand jury investigation. Jurors left the courthouse and declined to speak to the press.

The conviction is a vindication for the Justice Department, which overcame attempts by Huawei to derail the case before trial and had to navigate years of delays because of the Covid pandemic, which made it difficult for lawyers and witnesses to travel. Along the way, two Chinese intelligence officers were accused in 2022 of trying to bribe a US law enforcement official with US$61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and get inside information about the case.

Huawei now faces fines, forfeiture and restitution but the US has not specified the scope of financial penalties it will seek at sentencing, which is scheduled for September 2027.

From the beginning, the Huawei case heightened tensions between Washington and Beijing while the world’s two largest economies were mired in a trade war. Months later, officials in Donald Trump’s administration labelled the company a national security threat, alleging that it sold telecommunications equipment that could be used by China’s Communist Party for spying.

The initial criminal indictment set off a diplomatic crisis when Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou, whose father founded the company, was arrested at the behest of the US on financial fraud charges while travelling through Canada. Almost three years after Meng was held under house arrest in Vancouver, she reached a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021 that allowed her to return to China, but after she admitted that the company violated US sanctions by illegally conducting business in Iran.

title: Europe is beating Asia in fight for gas supply disrupted by war
article:
(Nov 25): Europe’s rush for liquefied natural gas is playing out in the Atlantic Ocean, where high prices are drawing tankers carrying the vital industrial and power-station fuel away from Asia.

Eight vessels with LNG from the US Gulf Coast have changed course to Europe so far this month, according to data intelligence firm Kpler. That is the most since the Middle East war cut off Qatari exports from the global market in late February, making the US the world’s dominant supplier of the super-chilled fuel.

Europe has been aided by relatively weak demand in Asia, allowing it to draw in more gas to limit the drain on inventories that are already at record lows for this time of year. LNG prices in Europe surged to a four-year high last month and that has helped shut the so-called “arb” — the premium that typically lures American gas across the Pacific to China and Japan. Europe is now paying more than Asia since the war began, according to Spark Commodities.

The continent’s success in pulling in cargoes is helping it to meet surging demand for gas as temperatures drop but the high prices that utilities are paying for shipments are already coursing through the economy. Energy-intensive industries like steel, fertilisers and chemicals are faced with steeply higher costs, and some factories are having to suspend operations when power prices get too high while the expensive gas will eventually flow through to household bills and inflation.

“Supply shortages are pulling LNG to the EU, and the profitable trade remains there,” said Carl Larry, an oil and gas analyst at energy consultancy Enverus. “Unfortunately, the EU is paying the premium.”

See also: Japan LNG buying poised to rise as gas power turns profitable

Europe has been able to turn around tankers in the Atlantic thanks in part to the world’s biggest buyers — China and Japan — remaining largely on the sidelines of the spot market. The two countries remain well supplied and have yet to see significant cold snaps that might prompt utilities there to bid for more gas. Northeast Asian inventories are likely sufficient for winter and the current high prices offer little incentive for spot purchases, Rystad Energy said in a note last week.

European imports have jumped more than 45% over the last three months on a 30-day moving average basis while deliveries to Northeast Asia are down about 1%, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Despite the increase, European Union and UK imports are still slightly lower than last year, an indication the region will need to buy more.

It is the opposite of what happened over the Northern Hemisphere summer when Asian countries — more vulnerable to the energy shock caused by the US-Iran war — competed more aggressively for LNG.

See also: Chinese refiners snapping up cut-price oil to refill stockpiles

That was behind Europe’s struggle to replenish inventories earlier this year so it would have enough over winter, when heating consumption pushes up overall LNG demand. EU storage tanks are now 68% full, compared to a five-year average of 86%, with withdrawals accelerating despite the higher imports.

“Europe has allowed itself to enter winter with extraordinary low stock levels,” said Saul Kavonic, an energy analyst at MST Marquee. “We are going to see increasing direct competition between Northeast Asia and Europe for LNG as winter progresses.”

The need for seaborne gas in Europe is intensifying as the region has been dealing with an early bout of cold, with wrong-footing pundits who had been expecting the El Niño weather pattern to bring milder temperatures. An extended freeze could result in Northwest Europe ending winter with inventories just 14% full, the lowest since 2018, Goldman Sachs Group Inc said in a note this week.

The wide European premium over Asia is likely to continue into the first quarter, especially as the region plans to ban imports of Russian LNG, according to Evan Tan, an LNG analyst at commodities intelligence firm ICIS. “Storage deficit, Russian LNG void and weather-driven demand will likely shut any arb to Asia,” he said.

There is also still a risk that a dip in temperatures in Asia could once again draw LNG away from Europe. Spot electricity prices have surged in Japan this month, making it affordable to import LNG for gas-fired power stations for the first time since February. Already, one Japanese utility has bought an LNG shipment for December delivery while selling a cargo for March, according to traders.

For now, outlooks for China, Japan and South Korea are pointing to milder-than-normal temperatures — at least in the short term. That could allow Europe to keep soaking up US LNG without a deeper price war with Asia, although predicting the weather remains a fickle business.

“Asia is only one cold spell or pickup in utility demand away from bidding it back in their favour," said Toby Copson, China-based managing partner at Davenport Energy, which trades oil and gas. “If that happens, we’ll see competition for spot cargoes pick up rapidly.”

title: Metals rout deepens as AI, Fed worries fuel bearish sentiment
article:
(Nov 25): Copper, aluminium and tin all added to Tuesday’s fierce selloff in metals as tech stocks extended losses and traders braced for US inflation data that will feed the Federal Reserve’s next moves on interest rates.

After muted early trading, prices on the London Metal Exchange moved decisively lower, with copper adding to a slump of more than 5% on Tuesday to reach its lowest level since December last year. Aluminium dropped as much as 1.6% and tin fell nearly 4%.

Metals have tumbled this month — despite some near-term supply tightness — in a rout fuelled by doubts over the artificial-intelligence boom, as well as the prospect of Fed hikes and mounting worries over softer consumption in China. There is also the threat of imminent trade action by the Trump administration.

“The price declines reflect concerns about downward revisions to AI-related capital spending,” said Li Xuezhi, head of research at brokerage Chaos Ternary Futures Co. “Combined with weak domestic demand in China, this is also likely to lead to lower estimates for global aggregate demand.”

Copper, in particular, has been swept up in the bearish turn for AI stocks, after optimism about demand from data centres helped carry the metal to a record near US$15,000 a tonne in September. Should copper end the month near its latest levels, November will go down as one of the metal’s worst months on record.

See also: LME to list major new aluminium brand as historic squeeze deepens

Technology shares have extended declines this week after a brief bounce on Monday that followed Jensen Huang’s unexpected return to head chipmaker Nvidia Corp. following a scandal.

Three-month copper fell 0.7% to US$11,743 a tonne on the LME by 4.04pm in Singapore, while aluminium dropped 1.1% to US$2,739 a tonne. Tin, which is also closely tied to the AI theme, shed 7.3% on Tuesday, then 2.9% in the midweek session to US$38,400 a tonne.

See also: China extends pause on US minerals ban to maintain truce

Metals are falling even as buyers scramble to get hold of prompt supplies, signalled by steep backwardations on futures markets and rising physical premiums. Nearby spreads on aluminium narrowed significantly later on Tuesday after the LME unleashed rule changes to cope with an intensifying squeeze on nearby positions.

The LME’s main mechanism to address squeezes — known as its "Tom-next lending rules" — now applies to those with positions equal to more than 30% of available aluminium stockpiles, down from 50%. The exchange also tightened lending requirements for traders holding major positions for longer than five days.

The squeeze prompted the head of major aluminium maker Norsk Hydro ASA to air concerns.

“For us as a producer, and for our consumers, it is imperative that the LME is a relevant and well-functioning exchange,” CEO Eivind Kallevik said in a Bloomberg TV interview. “The worst thing is when you have intermittent or rapid changes” that can create confusion and uncertainty, he said.

Aluminium's key cash-to-three-month spread fell to US$67.53 a tonne on Tuesday, down from more than US$400 on Monday.

Investors will also be watching the Fed’s preferred gauge of inflation, personal consumption expenditure, which is due later Wednesday (Nov 25). Investors have already fully priced in a quarter-point rate increase next month. The Trump administration could also announce plans for new tariffs on China and other major economies, which has the potential to spook the market.

“The fact that prices continued to slump despite the absence of any new negative catalysts suggests that the selloff was driven more by sentiment than fundamentals,” said Michael Wu, base metals derivatives trader at Jiangsu Xinbu New Materials Technology Group. “We probably shouldn’t be this pessimistic.”

title: Maybank reviews portfolio as chip curbs hit data centres
article:
(Nov 25): Malaysia’s largest bank is reviewing its portfolio for potential exposure to the latest US chip curbs, as it assesses how the restrictions could affect data centre clients and their funding needs.

“There is an increased level of scrutiny that is obviously required, given the new developments and the new policies affecting the compute financing,” Michael Oh-Lau, chief executive officer of Maybank Investment Bank Bhd, said in an interview with Bloomberg TV’s Haslinda Amin.

Maybank will get clarity from its clients to ensure “they’re still well positioned to proceed with the financing requirements that they have”, he said.

Lenders are launching sweeping reviews of data centre projects in the wake of tougher rules to curb Chinese companies’ use of advanced US chips in Southeast Asian nations. Banks from Citigroup Inc to Standard Chartered plc are pressing clients for further details on who uses their chips and seeking proof they’re in line with stricter export-control rules enacted by the US Commerce Department, Bloomberg reported Wednesday.

Though there’s little public data, analysts estimate anywhere from 30%-45% of Malaysia’s data centre capacity is linked to Chinese demand. While data centres also serve local and Western clients, the fastest-growing and more lucrative segment has been Chinese firms needing overseas access to advanced chips for artificial intelligence (AI) training.

Estimates by Natixis SA show that Southeast Asian banks are the second largest source of funding for China-linked data centres, after Chinese lenders. Banks in the region, especially Singapore and Malaysia, will likely take a hit from the latest chip curbs, Natixis said in a report on Monday.

See also: Banks put data centre clients under microscope on AI chips — Bloomberg

“Investors will need to recalibrate and adjust to the new norm,” Oh-Lau said. Still, he expects strong investment momentum to continue into 2027.

Malaysia’s economy has expanded above expectations for much of the year, supported by resilient domestic spending and demand linked to AI, which has fuelled semiconductor exports and a surge in data-centre investment. Officials are assessing the potential impact of new US restrictions on growth, though the central bank governor predicted that the tech upcycle will be sustained into next year.

Oh-Lau sees a strong pipeline of initial public offerings for 2027 following a blowout year for new share sales this year as more local companies reach scale. He expects some standout listings in the healthcare and technology sectors.

See also: Trump threatens to tax firms building data centres abroad

While geopolitical shocks and sharp movements in rates and currencies may affect sentiment, Oh-Lau said investors are beginning to see Malaysia as a defensive market against risk.

“We’ve never been this busy,” Oh-Lau said of 2026, adding that “Malaysia is a good place to be.”

title: Market convulsions create a US$375 bil winner: India
article:
(Nov 25): Indian stocks extended their world-beating November rally and the rupee hit an eight-month high versus the dollar as renewed selling in the artificial intelligence trade spurred demand for the nation’s assets.

The NSE Nifty 50 Index soared as much as 2.4% on Wednesday, while Asian equities slumped, tracking declines in US technology stocks as investors questioned whether lofty AI valuations and massive spending plans can be sustained. Taiwan and South Korea, among the markets most dominated by AI, led declines in the region.

The MSCI India index has added nearly US$375 billion ($484.3 billion) in market value this month, as a market long shunned for its lack of AI plays emerges as a bright spot for global investors. Stock benchmarks in India have rallied more than 12% in November, beating more than 90 major global equity indexes tracked by Bloomberg.

“India has been an underperformer over the past two years simply because it lacks AI exposure. But at this moment, this has become a merit,” Dong Chen, chief investment officer for Asia at Bank J Safra Sarasin, said on Bloomberg Television.

The rotation has brought foreign investors back. Global funds have poured nearly US$14 billion into local equities in November, a monthly record, after withdrawing unprecedented sums earlier this year. Their comeback has made the rupee the top emerging-market currency this quarter, after hitting a record low against the greenback in early October.

See also: Asian stocks fall as AI trade falters, gold drops

The currency rallied as much as 0.8% to 92.18 per dollar on Wednesday, its strongest level since March 12.

“INR is benefitting from lower oil prices and a rotation out of AI-heavy markets and into Indian equities, as reflected in strong foreign portfolio inflows,” said Lloyd Chan, a currency strategist in MUFG Bank Ltd. in Singapore. “Recent RBI measures to support FX have also helped.”

Goldman Sachs Group Inc and HSBC Holdings Plc have upgraded their outlook on Indian stocks as sentiment improves, while others including Morgan Stanley remain on the sidelines. Morgan Stanley is equal-weight on the market.

See also: Asian stocks jump as Huang’s return lifts AI trade

Nomura Holdings Inc also sees limited upside after the rally pushed equity valuations higher. The Nifty trades at 18.8 times one-year forward earnings, up from a low of 16.5 times, while its premium to US and emerging-market equities is at a four-year high.

Still, strategists remain broadly bullish on the India heading into 2027, citing earnings momentum.

Investors have thought of India as more of an “anti-AI trade,” but “corporate earnings have been tracking pretty well as well,” Christina Woon, a portfolio manager at Eastspring Investments SP Ltd, told Bloomberg TV.

title: German economic growth revised down as investment sinks
article:
(Nov 25): Germany’s economy expanded at a slower pace than first thought in the third quarter as investment slumped.

Gross domestic product rose 0.1% between July and September, less than the 0.2% preliminary reading, the statistics office said Wednesday (Nov 25). While government spending jumped 0.3% from the previous three months and private consumption increased 0.1%, capital investment sank 1.2%.

The economy is still on track for its best year since 2022 after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government launched a vast public-spending drive to shore up infrastructure and defence capabilities.

Exports, the country’s traditional growth driver, also played a key role in the first half of the year as companies benefited from the global investment boom in artificial intelligence. The pharmaceutical industry probably saw extra demand before new US tariffs and chemical firms got a temporary boost from the Iran war hurting Asian competitors.

That changed in the third quarter as goods exports fell 0.8%, driven by decreases in cars, chemicals and metals, Destatis said. Imports dropped even more strongly, however.

See also: Eurozone activity holds steady as Germany offsets French slump

Michael Herzum, an economist at Union Investment, said private investment remains the weak point of Germany’s recovery.

“The high level of geopolitical uncertainty during the summer months dampened companies’ willingness to invest,” he said in a statement, adding it’s crucial that firms resume doing so to expand production.

Commerzbank chief economist Joerg Kraemer said the development shows companies’ disappointment about the government’s inability to enact economic reforms.

See also: French companies to announce €14.9 bil in investments

The Bundesbank has said activity will pick up again in the final quarter as exports regain momentum. Overall, the government’s economic advisers expect 1.3% expansion in GDP this year followed by 1% in 2027.

title: UK energy bills rise 26% as war fuels cost-of-living squeeze
article:
(Nov 25): UK households are set for a sharp rise in energy costs in January as the Middle East war pushes up wholesale gas and electricity prices, with winter demand adding further pressure.

Ofgem’s price cap, which limits how much suppliers can charge consumers per unit of energy, will rise 26% to £2,166 (US$2,833) from Jan 1, the watchdog said in a statement on Wednesday. This is the steepest rise since October 2022, at the height of Europe’s energy crisis following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The increase adds to the cost-of-living squeeze as the war in Iran pushes up inflation and borrowing costs across the economy. It also threatens to erode government efforts to ease pressure on households, while strained public finances leave ministers with limited room to cushion the blow.

“For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets,” Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said in a statement.

The price households will pay for each unit of gas they use jumped 38% from the previous cap to a record, surpassing even the level seen at the height of the last energy crisis.

See also: YTL PowerSeraya targets more commercial customers while maintaining leading position in residential market

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has sought to shield homes by cutting VAT on energy costs, while ministers added further support in the October Budget, including a £100 payment for millions of households. This latest increase risks swallowing up much of that relief.

Bills are expected to remain above £2,000 throughout 2027, according to forecasts from energy consultancy Cornwall Insight Ltd, with prices forecast to fall just 1% when the cap changes again in April. Wholesale energy prices have surged since the US-Iran war began earlier this year, with UK gas futures and power contracts more than doubling.

“We would love to be able to point to a moment when the outlook will turn around, but the honest answer is that it depends on what happens in the Middle East,” said Craig Lowrey, retail markets principal at Cornwall Insight.

See also: Coal miners need their rivals to go bust

The surge in energy prices has already pushed inflation to 3.6%, the highest level in a year. Officials raised interest rates in November for the first time in more than three years to prevent price pressures from spreading across the economy, and markets expect another hike at the December meeting.

The price rise will start to feed through to the broader economy next year. The cap is fixed for three months, locking in higher energy costs through the winter and contributing to Bloomberg Economics’ expectation that inflation will accelerate further.

Higher prices for longer will deepen the strain on vulnerable homes that has persisted since the 2022 energy shock. Many households are already struggling to pay their bills, and domestic energy debt reached a record £5 billion in the second quarter, almost double its level three years earlier.

title: Spain’s Indra targets more than €12 bil in 2030 revenue
article:
(Nov 25): Spanish defence and technology company Indra Sistemas SA raised its guidance on Wednesday (Nov 25) as new chairman Ángel Simón unveiled his strategy after a management shake-up earlier this year.

Indra said it now expects revenue of more than €12 billion by 2030 and a slightly higher margin than before. The company previously targeted €10 billion in 2030, though management said in February that it expected to reach that level sooner.

The Madrid-based company also raised its 2026 revenue guidance to €7 billion from €6 billion. Shares rose as much as 7% at market open in Madrid. They were up 6.3% to €55.32 at 10.05am.

The investor day is the first under Simón and chief executive Josep María Recasens, who took up their roles this year after a reorganisation at the top of the partly state-owned group.

The new plan “extends Indra’s strong growth trajectory, supported by high backlog visibility and a conservative assumption on Spanish defence spending,” Mediobanca analysts including Alessandro Pozzi said.

Simón replaced Ángel Escribano in April after weeks of tensions over the company’s direction and pressure from the government, which wields influence over Indra through state holding company Sepi, its largest shareholder. The new strategy is being presented just days before Spain’s Nov 29 general election.

See also: Huawei found guilty of US criminal charges in landmark case

Under the new plan, Indra is also shifting away from building as much as possible in-house while retaining the industrial footprint expanded under former chairman Escribano. The company expects defence margins to fall to 16% from 18% as it takes on more prime-contractor programmes and relies more on suppliers to deliver its backlog, according to Wednesday’s presentation.

Indra has been one of the beneficiaries of a sharp increase in Spanish and European military spending, with the company’s defence revenue doubling in the first nine months of 2026 and its overall order backlog up 133% year-on-year as of September.

The strategy follows the collapse earlier this year of Indra’s proposed acquisition of Escribano Mechanical & Engineering, the defence manufacturer controlled by Escribano and his brother Javier, after the deal drew scrutiny over potential conflicts of interest.

See also: Asia data centre sound out US clients to replace China demand

The new strategy also comes as Spain’s anti-corruption prosecutor investigates allegations of irregularities in the award of some government defence contracts involving Indra and Escribano Mechanical & Engineering, the company controlled by Ángel Escribano and his brother Javier.

title: China, US set for ‘new chapter’ of trade talks, ex-official says
article:
(Nov 25): China and the US will make more headway once their trade talks resume in January, when their year-old tariff truce is set to expire, according to a former top Chinese economic official.

“They will open a new chapter and make trade relations between China and the US more healthy,” Zhu Guangyao, who was China’s vice minister of finance from 2010 to 2018, said in an interview with Bloomberg TV in Singapore on Wednesday. While “some differences” may remain, he said the negotiators will “continue to talk and make that progress step by step.”

His upbeat comments follow days after President Donald Trump’s visit to Shenzhen for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping during a gathering of Asia Pacific economies. Both Xi and Trump appeared to lean heavily on their personal rapport to keep ties between their countries on an even keel, even as fresh strains have emerged between the world’s biggest economies, including an alleged spy scandal involving involving Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang.

Zhu served as deputy finance minister until his retirement in 2018, overseeing the Customs Tariff Department and playing a key role in US-China trade negotiations.

As soon as on Tuesday, the US is set to announce plans to raise tariffs on goods from countries including China, as the Trump administration moves to replace levies struck down by the Supreme Court.

The duties are expected to target economies accused of hurting American industry by subsidizing their domestic manufacturers, Bloomberg News has reported. The tariffs on Chinese products are expected to be broader in nature than charges on items from others and will lack exemptions, though they will be within the bounds of the trade ceasefire President Xi Jinping reached with his US counterpart, Donald Trump, last year in South Korea.

See also: Starbucks said to engage banks for sale of Japan business — Bloomberg

Zhu said that issues arising from Washington’s investigation into excess manufacturing capacity under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act can be settled through negotiations.

title: IOI Properties defends Malaysian REIT IPO pricing as parent trades 40% below book, sees room for upside
article:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 25): IOI Properties Group Bhd (KL:IOIPG) on Wednesday defended the pricing of the initial public offering (IPO) of its real estate investment trust (REIT), saying the listing let the developer monetise its assets at book value while its own shares trade at about a 40% discount.

IOI Properties group chief executive officer and IOIPG Malaysia REIT (KL:IOIREIT) executive chairman Datuk Lee Yeow Seng said the final IPO price of 91 sen per unit matches the trust’s pro forma net asset value (NAV) per unit.

He added that the group had also chosen to leave room for potential upside for investors instead of maximising the IPO price.

“Currently, IOI Properties is actually priced at about 40% below book value, so we actually are able to create value by listing IOIPG Malaysia REIT at book value,” he told reporters at a press conference following the REIT’s listing ceremony on Wednesday.

“We don’t want to price the IPO to the maximum, where there’s no upside and nothing left on the table for the investors,” he added.

IOIPG Malaysia REIT’s final IPO price was set at 91 sen per unit, 5.2% below the initial indicative retail price of 96 sen.

See also: IOIPG Malaysia REIT opens lower in trading debut

The Malaysian public portion of the IPO, the largest-ever REIT listing in Malaysia, was oversubscribed by just 0.59 times.

Maybank Investment Bank Bhd regional head of equity capital markets Raymond Chooi, meanwhile, clarified that the indicative retail price of 96 sen stated in the prospectus was the top of the pricing range, and that the final offer price was determined through the bookbuilding exercise.

“It was never set at 96 sen to begin with. It is a maximum price because in a bookbuilding process, there is never certainty. And that (process) also provides us some flexibility in terms of pricing the REIT,” he said.

See also: DayOne said to pause US IPO plans on data center, market concerns — Bloomberg

Chooi said the final price of 91 sen took into account prevailing market sentiment and feedback from investors, while ensuring that the valuation was acceptable to the issuer.

Maybank Investment Bank and AmInvestment Bank Bhd are the joint principal advisers and joint global coordinators for the IPO.

IPO proceeds to fund debt repayment, capex and acquisitions at sponsor level

The IPO, which was structured entirely as an offer for sale of existing units, raised about RM2 billion ($626.7 million) for IOI Properties, with no fresh capital raised by the REIT itself.

Meanwhile, IOI Properties shareholders were entitled to purchase one REIT unit for every 10 existing IOIPG ordinary shares held.

When asked about the decision against issuing new units to raise funds for the REIT, IOIPG Malaysia REIT head of finance Alvin Loo said IOI Properties had already earmarked the proceeds from the listing exercise for its own funding requirements, including debt repayment, capital expenditure and acquisitions.

“For us, we have already earmarked the proceeds from this REIT exercise to repay some of our borrowing, and also this will be utilised for the capital expenditure that we already anticipated, including some of the acquisitions that we have at the sponsor level,” he said.
