IOIPG Malaysia REIT has an initial portfolio of nine properties valued at RM7.66 billion, comprising IOI City Mall in Putrajaya, six hotels operating under Marriott International’s brands and two office developments

Separately, Lee said IOI Properties is working on a proposal for its board’s approval for a secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX), which the property developer is targeting to undertake in 2027.

“We are targeting around next year. If anything, we need to table it to the board first for approval,” he said.

“Currently, the management is working on the groundwork to prepare a proposal to be brought forward to the board.”

IOI Properties had previously disclosed that it had begun engaging the SGX over a potential secondary listing.

The property developer has a sizeable presence in Singapore, with assets including IOI Central Boulevard Towers in the city-state’s central business district and the South Beach integrated development.

At the time of writing, shares in IOI Properties were trading down one sen or 0.34% at RM2.90, valuing the property developer at RM17.56 billion. Meanwhile, IOIPG Malaysia REIT was trading down three sen or 3.3% at 88 sen, with a market capitalisation of RM4.84 billion.

title: Asia data centre sound out US clients to replace China demand
article:
(Nov 25): Data centres across Asia are racing to offload excess computing power to US buyers after the Trump administration tightened a loophole that gave Chinese tech firms access to Nvidia Corp’s most advanced chips.

That’s according to Ronit Jain, chief executive and co-founder of Liquid Compute, a New York-based startup building a regulated exchange for AI computing capacity. A new rule targeting exports of cutting-edge AI accelerators to the region is hitting data centre providers that were counting on renting computational resources to Chinese customers, he said.

The cost to access Nvidia’s powerful B300 graphics processing units was US$7.72 per GPU-hour at the end of last month, according to a Liquid Compute index. That had fallen 7% to US$7.19 as of Tuesday, according to the startup, which says it tracks over 200 data centre companies. A post Jain made on X last week highlighting the declining prices drew widespread attention.

“All the neoclouds based in Asia-Pacific selling to Tencent and other companies, or in Singapore or Taiwan with Chinese companies as offtakers, have excess capacity,” Jain said in an interview. “They’re trying to broker it into the US.” He declined to name the companies selling their excess compute, or the buyers.

I would expect B300 pricing to continue declining.

A staggering number of neoclouds have approached us @liquidcompute looking to remarket long-term B300 capacity originally committed to Chinese-affiliated offtakers into the US and Western Europe due to concerns of stricter… — Ronit Jain (@ronitrjain) November 19, 2026

This time last year, the price of B300s stood at US$4.55 per GPU-hour and had steadily increased before falling over the course of the last month, Jain said.

See also: Huawei found guilty of US criminal charges in landmark case

Nvidia’s board reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive officer this week, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations that he’d had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman the US government has investigated for spying on behalf of China. At the heart of the scandal was the woman’s company, Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which was alleged to have been smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China.

The US government last week said shipments of advanced chips to four countries in Southeast Asia will require Washington’s permission. It also announced a soon-to-come global clampdown on data centres that provide Chinese firms with remote access to advanced hardware they’re restricted from buying.

New York-based Liquid Compute, which was founded in 2024, tracks over 200 neoclouds, many of them with operations in Asia-Pacific, Jain said. In September, the startup raised US$15 million in a seed round co-led by FirstMark Capital and Chemistry Ventures. The company is also backed by startup accelerator Y Combinator.

See also: Ex-RBI chief Rajan sees Nvidia governance risk with return of Huang

Before the controversy, Nvidia’s Huang had been among the most vocal advocates of Chinese chip buying. Even with his reinstatement, market participants appear to be operating under the assumption that Chinese firms will no longer be able to access Nvidia’s chips via AI cloud providers, according to Jain.

“Just based on basic economics, you would expect the price to decrease with a temporary influx of supply,” he said.

title: Bitcoin funds head for worst month as outflows near US$5 bil
article:
(Nov 25): US-listed exchange-traded funds investing in bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent selloff in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away.

A net US$4.71 billion has been withdrawn from the funds in November so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg through Nov 23. BlackRock Inc.’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions this month, also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow.

The exodus comes as bitcoin tumbles below US$60,000 and heads for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, when a string of corporate failures triggered a broader crypto-market meltdown. The token has dropped about 23% this month and was trading around US$59,200 as of 1pm Wednesday in Singapore, down about 1% in the Asia session.

The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024. The funds opened the cryptocurrency to a wider pool of institutional and retail investors and became an important source of demand during the bull market. Their record redemptions are now reinforcing the current downturn as that source of buying dries up.

Bitcoin briefly recovered alongside other risk assets on Monday after Nvidia Corp reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, but has since surrendered all of those gains, a sign that investors are using rallies to reduce exposure.

See also: Bitcoin fails to hold Nvidia bump with crypto headwinds in focus

“When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note. “Bitcoin trades around the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.”

Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds at the moment, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following recent US midterm elections. The absence of US demand is adding to the pressure, according to Glassnode.

See also: Bitcoin ETF exodus gathers pace, removing key source of support

“The ETFs and other institutions were an important source of demand on the way up, and there is little interest from them at these prices,” the firm said. “A return to ETF inflows, together with net buying on Coinbase, would be the first sign that this is changing.”

Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates toward equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management.

Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now,” Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning.”

The cryptocurrency industry may need a fresh catalyst to revive demand after the forces that drove the previous rally have faded, she said.

“I think we do need to find a new narrative, a new catalyst, a new market, something new for the entire industry for us to become that emerging asset class again,” Kiani said. “There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point. So, like, why bitcoin?”

title: Malaysia’s EPF to boost overseas stakes, likes infrastructure
article:
(Nov 25): Malaysia’s largest pension fund aims to increase its overseas investments to 50% in five to six years as it repositions its RM1.5 trillion (US$365 billion) portfolio in an environment of higher stock valuations and bond yields and heightened geopolitical uncertainty, its chief executive officer said.

“That’s where I see the portfolio going,” Employee Provident Fund CEO Ahmad Zulqarnain Onn said in an interview with Bloomberg Television’s Haslinda Amin on Wednesday. Currently, the state-run mandatory retirement savings fund for private sector workers has 38% of its total portfolio invested overseas.

The fund favours investing in infrastructure, Ahmad said, adding that trends around AI, digitisation and energy transition are driving a lot of infrastructure spending.

One of Asia’s largest retirement funds, EPF manages RM1.5 trillion in assets for its more than 16 million members. In the last ten years, EPF has paid an average annual dividend of about 5.9%, more than double the 2.7% earnings from Malaysian banks’ one-year fixed deposits over the same period.

title: Starbucks said to engage banks for sale of Japan business — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 25): Starbucks Corp has tapped advisers to prepare for a potential sale of its Japan business for several billion dollars, according to people familiar with the matter.

The US coffee chain is working with banks including Citigroup Inc and Morgan Stanley and has started sounding out interest from some strategic and financial investors, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t public. A formal process might start as soon as this year, they said.

Starbucks has about 2,000 coffeehouses in Japan, making it one of the company’s biggest markets. Deliberations about the business are ongoing and might not result in a sale, the people said.

A Starbucks spokesperson said the company continually assesses the best structure for its customers and creating value for shareholders. The chain has a strong business in Japan, where it’s been for more than 30 years, the spokesperson said.

Bloomberg News reported in June that Starbucks was considering options for the Japanese business and had held preliminary talks with banks.

See also: AI chip boom to see won build on best year in almost a decade

Starbucks doesn’t break out standalone revenue for Japan, but combined with Canada and the UK, the three accounted for about 72% of net revenues generated outside the US and China in fiscal 2026.

title: Shein to pay US$100 mil to end US deceptive marketing case
article:
(Nov 25): Shein Global Holdings Ltd agreed to pay US$100 million ($129 million) to resolve US Federal Trade Commission allegations that the Chinese fast-fashion retailer deceived consumers about its products, suppliers and consumer reviews.

In a complaint filed in California federal court, the FTC alleged Shein violated US consumer protection laws by failing to provide adequate customer service, illegally screening consumer reviews and misrepresenting the country of origin and labour practices of its suppliers. The antitrust and consumer protection agency seeks an injunction and monetary relief for consumers harmed by the company’s allegedly illegal practices.

The terms of the settlement, including the US$100 million payment, which will be used to reimburse consumers, were also filed in federal court.

In a statement, the company said it had reached an agreement to resolve the investigation, which it said related to “certain historical business practices”. The company also said that it disagrees with the FTC’s characterisations, but was taking steps to bolster its compliance practices.

Shares of Shein opened largely flat on Wednesday morning in Hong Kong.

For years, Shein had no customer service phone number and, until September 2025, only five agents despite selling millions of packages to the US every day, the FTC said. The company also delayed or refused to publish consumer reviews that contained what it deemed “unhelpful words” such as “damaged”, “bad quality”, “very disappointed” and “waste of money” among others, according to the complaint.

The agency also alleged that Shein failed to substantiate its marketing claims about responsible sourcing or the use of cotton grown by forced labour.

Shein, which had shares listed in Hong Kong on Sept 1, has attracted millions of shoppers in the US and Europe with rock-bottom prices and a torrent of new styles by capitalising on customs duty waivers for small-value parcels. The Trump administration has sought to close that loophole, ending the so-called de minimis exemption that allowed cheap goods to pass through customs tariff-free for nearly 90 years.

Shein’s US sales fell 6.6% in the 12-month period that ended in October, according to Bloomberg Second Measure, which analyses credit and debit card transactions.

See also: Onitsuka Tiger pivots from Asics stripes to tap luxury market

The latest case adds to a growing list of legal and regulatory challenges for Shein in the US. Its purchase of American clothing retailer Everlane triggered a national security review by US authorities earlier this year. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued the company in February, alleging that it unlawfully sold toxic products and exposed Americans’ personal data to the Chinese government.

The retailer has also drawn scrutiny in Western markets over its environmental and labour practices, including cotton tied to China’s Xinjiang region.

Its handling of customer data has come under pressure too. French regulators last year fined Shein roughly €150 million (US$164 million or $212 million) for violating online tracking rules, including by placing advertising cookies on users’ devices without their consent.

Shein’s expansion beyond fashion has brought further headaches. In late 2025, the company came under scrutiny over childlike sex dolls and weapons sold on its third-party marketplace, prompting investigations in France and leaving it at risk of hefty EU penalties. The controversy coincided with strong political pushback to the opening of its first physical store in Paris.

title: AI chip boom to see won build on best year in almost a decade
article:
(Nov 25): South Korea’s AI chip windfall is unleashing a wave of year-end currency flows, potentially pushing the won into its next phase of gains.

SK Hynix Inc and Samsung Electronics Co are poised to convert much of their massive export earnings to pay for dividends and record employee bonuses in won. They will also need more of the local currency to cover large tax bills owed to the government from the artificial intelligence hardware surge.

Those inflows are expected to help boost the won into the 1,200-per-dollar range by the end of the first half of 2027, according to Macro Hive and Korea Investment & Securities. Citing similar catalysts, Goldman Sachs Group Inc sees the currency strengthening to 1,280 next year, a roughly 5% gain from Wednesday’s level of 1,345.80.

Compressed into the next few weeks, these payouts bode well for the won, adding momentum to a 7% gain against the dollar so far this year. While overseas investors repatriating their dividends may create some won-selling pressure in the short term, record exports and a hefty current-account surplus also keep the currency’s 2027 upward trajectory intact, market watchers say.

“The bigger story is that exporters still have substantial dollar-selling needs,” said Vivek Rajpal, Asia strategist at JB Drax Honore in Singapore. “The won’s appreciation trend has further to go despite weak sentiment towardsAI stocks.”

See also: Alibaba in talks for potential yuan, dollar bond sale next year — Bloomberg

The won has rallied about 16% since hitting a 17-year low in June, as exporters led by chipmakers stepped up dollar sales to fund projects in Korea. The currency is outperforming all its Asian peers this year and heading for its biggest annual gain since 2017.

Korea’s two largest chipmakers are rolling out unprecedented dividend plans, driven by a memory-chip sales bonanza and a government push for local firms to boost shareholder returns.

Samsung is scheduled to distribute 30 trillion won (US$22.3 billion) in third-quarter cash dividends on Nov 27, which is about 12 times the average size of its quarterly payouts since the beginning of 2025, according to filings.

See also: Foxconn faces India insolvency lawsuit over unpaid vendor dues — Bloomberg

SK Hynix will pay its 14.1 trillion won dividend allocation for the quarter roughly by the end of the year, or more than 50 times the average size of its quarterly payouts since the beginning of 2025, company filings show.

The payouts should support the won, said Moon Dawoon, an economist at Korea Investment & Securities. Companies are likely to convert more dollars into won to fund the payouts than what will ultimately flow back out as foreign investors repatriate their proceeds, she said.

To be sure, a large share of the cash will go to overseas shareholders, who tend to swiftly convert payouts back into greenbacks.

Foreign investors are estimated to receive about 15 trillion won from Samsung, while SK Hynix’s foreign investors are also slated to receive about half of its total payouts, according to Bloomberg calculations based on share ownership data.

In total, Samsung’s foreign investors will repatriate about half of the dividends they receive, amounting to about $5 billion, as they’ve typically done in the past, estimated Lee Minhyeok, an economist at Kookmin Bank.

Those outflows could bite harder toward year-end as global funds close their books and average trading volumes thin, a backdrop compounded by a stronger dollar and a pullback in semiconductor stocks, Lee said.

“There is considerable downside pressure” on the won this week ahead of the payouts, Lee said, referring to those from Samsung due Nov 27. “Some investors may convert their proceeds into dollars more quickly than usual to lock in their returns,” he added, while still expecting the won to rally in the longer-term period.

The chip boom is also set to deliver record worker bonuses early next year, potentially prompting chipmakers to sell more dollars to fund the won payouts.

Major chip, auto and shipbuilding companies will pay 60 trillion to 70 trillion won in bonuses in 2027, roughly six times this year’s 10.9 trillion won, according to Bank of Korea’s estimates.

Samsung and SK Hynix typically pay annual incentives in the first quarter, and the central bank estimated they alone will account for about 60 trillion won in the first three months of the year.

Bonus payments are likely to generate some temporary volatility in won trading, said Mingze Wu, a currency trader at StoneX Financial. “But overall the prevalent trend of the day will likely stay,” Wu added. Bonuses and special payments are “likely to be spaced out.”

Companies with December fiscal years must pay corporate taxes by the end of March, forcing exporters to raise won ahead of the deadline.

Thanks to a semiconductor-driven windfall, the Korean government projects record corporate tax revenue of 478.6 trillion won for 2026, up 28% from last year. Tax payments will contribute about $102 billion in net won demand and help lift the currency to 1,200 per dollar by mid-2027, Macro Hive estimates.

The chipmakers’ taxes and bonuses will be “a big deal,” JB Drax’s Rajpal said.

title: Alibaba in talks for potential yuan, dollar bond sale next year — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 25): Chinese e-commerce and cloud services giant Alibaba Group Holding Ltd has been in discussions in recent weeks with banks about potentially raising money in the offshore bond markets next year, people familiar with the matter said.

The company has held initial talks with investment banks to evaluate a potential sale of notes possibly in offshore yuan and dollars, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. Deliberations are preliminary and details could change. Borrowers weigh factors including market volatility in ultimately deciding on the timing for any offerings.

The group would join a growing number of tech firms that have been tapping capital markets to raise the trillions of dollars needed to finance AI infrastructure, testing how far investor demand can go. In October, Chinese technology and gaming company Tencent Holdings Ltd raised almost US$5.7 billion from the sale of bonds in yuan and dollars to support its growing investments in artificial intelligence.

Ahead of any potential overseas bond deal, Alibaba has been working on getting a quota for such issuance from the National Development and Reform Commission, the people said.

See also: Foxconn faces India insolvency lawsuit over unpaid vendor dues — Bloomberg

The company reported quarterly earnings last week, revealing an acceleration in capital expenditures to sustain its AI ambitions. Despite having successfully raised US$10.2 billion through a record-breaking Hong Kong share placement in August, its capital spending for the third quarter rose 60% from a year ago to about 50.5 billion yuan (US$7.6 billion), driven by faster computing scaling and the hardware buildout required for its Qwen AI models and expected AI agent adoption.The company has said it’s facing higher costs for chip components, a direct side effect of navigating US export controls and restricted supply chains. To counter these hardware bottlenecks, Alibaba had committed more than US$53 billion over a three-year period to build a full suite of services and businesses from models to chips.

To fund its push for semiconductor independence, Alibaba plans to list its chip-design unit, T-Head, in Hong Kong. The spinoff would give T-Head direct access to capital markets to develop domestic alternatives to US hardware.

title: Asian stocks fall as AI trade falters, gold drops
article:
(Nov 25): Asian stocks retreated after a sell-off in US technology shares revived doubts about the durability of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, extending losses from Wall Street into the region. Gold fell.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index slipped 2%, giving up some gains from Tuesday’s rally that was the biggest since July. The Kospi Index in South Korea lost 4.5% and the Taiwanese benchmark 5% as the two key barometers of the AI trade in Asia came under pressure. Futures for the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 indices both fell at least 0.4%.

Precious metals sold off as gold fell for a seventh time in eight sessions to around US$3,550 an ounce. Treasuries added to gains from the New York session when investors sought the safety of fixed income amid the losses in stocks. The yield on the benchmark 10-year note slipped one basis point to 4.92%.

The volatility in stocks underscore the uncertainty surrounding the AI trade as investors question whether massive technology spending can generate sufficient returns. Attention is now turning to Wednesday’s US inflation reading, which may affect the Federal Reserve’s policy path, and a possible tariff announcement from the Trump administration.

“This is so dizzying day to day,” said Adam Phillips, managing director of portfolio strategy at EP Wealth Advisors, who is not buying the dip in stocks yet. “Nothing has significantly changed from Monday, but we’re not out of the woods yet. There is still a whole lot of fear and uncertainty around the AI trade that needs to be worked through.”

Traders are parsing the Trump administration’s push to replace levies struck down by the Supreme Court. The US is set to announce as soon as late Tuesday in Washington plans to raise tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and more than a dozen other economies, according to people familiar with the matter.

See also: Asian stocks jump as Huang’s return lifts AI trade

The additional tariffs won’t push overall rates above levels agreed in individual trade deals, including pacts US President Donald Trump negotiated with the EU and China, people familiar with the details said. Still, the renewed focus on tariffs revived concerns about the potential impact on economic growth, corporate profits and inflation.

“The news of potential new US tariffs is probably mostly baked into market expectations at this point,” said Frederic Neumann, chief Asia economist at HSBC Holdings plc. “The US administration has been working for a while to replace some of the tariffs struck down by judges earlier this year, and its efforts have been well telegraphed.”

Investors remain focused on AI and the Fed into year-end, Neumann said.

See also: Asian stocks fall as Anthropic slips in after-hours

Stocks have swung back and forth in the past three sessions. Friday witnessed a selloff as the AI trade cratered, while equities bounced back on Monday as Jensen Huang returned to the helm of Nvidia Corp. Some of those gains were lost on Tuesday as Nvidia sank 5.9%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index tumbled 7.9% Tuesday, taking its decline from a June peak to about 40%. Anthropic PBC traded below its IPO price. Shares of Dell Technologies Inc and HP Inc edged up in extended trading after they issued upbeat forecasts.

“What the market is telling us is that investors do not believe that this amount of investment probably can proceed as they are guided previously, at least not in a sustainable way,” Dong Chen, chief investment officer Asia at Bank J Safra Sarasin, said on Bloomberg Television.

In other corners of the market, oil slipped as traders weighed signs of rising supply against escalating attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude fell 0.7% to US$90.75 a barrel.

Investors also parsed fresh US economic data that showed US consumer confidence surged to the highest in nearly two years. The report came ahead of the Fed’s preferred inflation metric, which is seen adding to bets that officials will raise interest rates in December.

Even as the Fed tightens policy, Treasuries will continue to advance over the next year, according to Joe Maher at Capital Economics.

“The tech-driven rout in the stock market has further to run and will prompt investors to revise down their rate expectations and trigger a ‘flight-to-safety’ into bonds,” he said.

title: Foxconn faces India insolvency lawsuit over unpaid vendor dues — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 25): About half a dozen vendors in India are experiencing payment delays by Foxconn Technology Group’s local unit, said people familiar with the matter, with one even filing an insolvency lawsuit to recover US$15 million in unpaid dues.

BCD Emprasa LLP, which leased dormitory housing in southern India for the Foxconn unit’s employees at the Bengaluru facility, has alleged that it didn’t receive payment for rent and utilities in an Aug 12 petition to the National Company Law Tribunal’s Chennai bench.

The company is seeking about 1.43 billion rupees (US$15.3 million) for past dues along with interest, service charges and damages as of July 8 from Foxconn Hon Hai Technology India Mega Development Pvt Ltd, according to the filing, which was seen by Bloomberg News.

Vendors in India often initiate insolvency proceedings to recover overdue payments, though these filings rarely push a company into bankruptcy.

While the dispute isn’t expected to derail Foxconn’s growth plans in India, it adds to the challenges facing the iPhone assembler as it competes with Tata Electronics Pvt Ltd for a bigger role in Apple Inc’s supply chain. Bloomberg News reported last year that Foxconn recalled hundreds of Chinese workers from India — though the reason wasn’t clear at the time — in a move that saw the company bring in staff from Taiwan and Vietnam to minimize the impact on production.

Foxconn didn’t reply to emailed queries seeking comments on BCD’s lawsuit in India.

See also: Intesa opens US$36 bil bid on world’s oldest bank to investors

“These defaults have caused grave financial prejudice and substantial commercial harm to the company” BCD said in an emailed response, adding that the matter was sub judice before NCLT.

At least four vendors other than BCD have been waiting for several months to over a year for Foxconn to clear their dues, said people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private information.

Several were hired for construction-related work on the Bengaluru facility and were working with Foxconn for the first time.

See also: Coca-Cola HBC rises in JSE debut ahead of US$2.6 bil deal

Under an April 2024 agreement with BCD, Foxconn leased 700 residential units for female employees, with rent payable regardless of occupancy and a lock-in through July 2026, according to the NCLT filing. Foxconn defaulted on an invoice due in May 2025, it said. The electronics giant also did not agree to appointing an arbitrator.

Departures of some non-Indian staff have slowed payments to local contractors, the people said.

title: Koh Eco’s subsidiary ordered to pay $30.1 mil to its joint venture partner following arbitration proceeding
article:
Back on Aug 18, Koh Brothers Eco’s (Koh Eco) wholly-owned subsidiary, Koh Brothers Building & Civil Engineering (KBCE) has commenced an arbitration proceeding against its joint venture partner, which is a construction and engineering company, in respect of a construction project.

Following which, the arbitral tribunal has issued its final award on Nov 24, which ordered KBCE to pay its joint venture partner a total amount of $30.1 million within 28 days.

With this development, Koh Eco is evaluating the various options with its legal advisors, including whether to ask the court to cancel or nullify the final award.

Nonetheless, Koh Eco expects the final award to have a material impact on its net tangible assets and earnings (loss) per share for FY2026 ending Dec 31.

“However, taking into account the overall financial position and liquidity, the board does out expect the final award to give rise to a material uncertainty that would cast significant doubt on the group's ability to continue as a going concern,” reads the Nov 25 announcement.

Koh Eco has been in the news recently following its Mainboard transfer, announcing plans to raise gross proceeds of up to $27.6 mil via rights issue at 4.9 cents each.

title: iX Biopharma aims to raise at least $14 mil by placing new shares at 39.8 cents each
article:
iX Biopharma announced it plans to raise at least $14 million by placing out roughly 35.18 million new shares at a placement price of 39.8 cents. The new shares represent around 3.1% of the enlarged share base.

At 39.8 cents, it represents a discount of 9% to the volume weighted average price of 43.72 cents for trades done on Nov 24.

iX Biopharma explains that the latest placement will provide funding to drive the development of Wafermine as well as the group’s expansion into the US through the compounding pharmacy pathway.

19% of the net proceeds will be allocated for the development and commercialisation of Wafermine while the remaining 33% will be used for general working capital.

title: Beng Kuang Marine CEO Yong lifts shareholding above 5%
article:
Beng Kuang Marine CEO Yong Jiunn Run has become a substantial shareholder of his company after exercising 3,045,000 warrants into new ordinary shares at an exercise price of $0.22 per share, for a total consideration of $669,900.

Yong now holds 5.09% interest in Beng Kuang, up from the previous 4.13%.

Beng Kuang executive chairman Chua Beng Yong says that he is “gratified” that Yong has increased his shareholding in Beng Kuang and further and aligning his interests closer with the firm’s shareholders.

Chua adds: “Since taking the helm as CEO, Yong has spearheaded a significant turnaround and strategic transformation of the group, delivering tangible results and enhancing value for shareholders. With the ‘Beng Kuang 2.0’ roadmap taking shape, I am confident that Yong’s leadership and commitment as both CEO and shareholder will continue to drive the group’s next phase of growth and value creation.”

Under Yong’s leadership and his “Beng Kuang 2.0” roadmap, Beng Kuang has achieved a turnaround, strengthening the balance sheet through non-core divestments, exiting underperforming businesses and reducing gearing.

The company has transformed its business model to focus on higher-growth, cash-generative infrastructure engineering and corrosion prevention services, becoming an asset-light and service-centric solutions provider specialised engineering, maintenance and regulatory compliance solutions for the marine and offshore energy sectors.

See also: Senior insiders spend on Wilmar, Mi Material and Stamford Land Corporation shares

Earnings quality has also improved, mostly coming from recurring FPSO lifecycle activities. The firm has consolidated subsidiary Asian Sealand Offshore and Marine while incubating new business opportunities to position the company for its next phase of growth.

More significantly, after returning to profitability in FY2023, shareholders were rewarded with the resumption of dividends and issuance of free warrants.

Shares in Beng Kuang closed at 29.5 cents on Nov 24, down 0.5 cents or 1.7%

title: Soaring US steel prices drive ‘mad scramble’ for imported tons
article:
(Nov 25) : Cheaper Asian imports are gaining traction with US steel buyers despite Washington’s tariffs, as a data center construction boom squeezes domestic supplies and drives up prices.

President Donald Trump’s 50% levies have sharply curtailed foreign steel shipments into the US. But with domestic prices of the metal reaching four-year highs, cheaper supply from East Asian sellers has flowed into the country in recent months.

Imports of South Korea’s flat-rolled steel surged 68% through October compared with the same period in 2025, according to data compiled by the American Iron and Steel Institute. October applications for steel from Vietnam more than doubled from September’s final import volumes, reaching 213,000 net tons and making it the fourth-largest foreign supplier that month.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and its needed power infrastructure has juiced up US demand for steel beyond expectations. The rush of projects — which use steel in anything from laying a building’s foundation to server racks and ductwork — is straining domestic supply, with steel orders booking up fast and US mills struggling to fulfill demand.

“There’s a mad scramble for tons,” said Timna Tanners, an analyst at Wells Fargo. “The US mills are not giving buyers enough steel — they’re cutting back on their supply agreements into 2027.”

The steady return of foreign imports reveals the limits of the Trump administration’s tariffs, which were designed to make foreign material prohibitively expensive and insulate domestic producers, like Nucor Corp., Steel Dynamics Inc. and Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. Persistent demand for steel has driven US prices to a height where foreign sellers can now afford the associated levies.

See also: Nasdaq 100 falls 2% on AI rout, tariff hike talk

Some imported steel can be nearly US$400 a ton cheaper than domestic supplies even after accounting for tariffs and shipping costs, according to a recent note from Jefferies analyst Albert Realini.

This week, Nucor, the largest American steel producer, raised its advertised price for hot-rolled coil to US$1,330 a short ton, extending a run of weekly increases that began during the summer. Hot-rolled coil, which is used to make products ranging from cars to construction materials, is the most widely traded form of steel.

Broader market prices have also climbed with US hot-rolled steel recently quoted at more than US$1,300 a ton, compared with less than US$900 a year earlier.

See also: US blacklists Megaspeed, and six firms across Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand over chip diversion risk

“Import volumes have been increasing in recent months, including a massive surge from South Korea,” Leon Topalian, Nucor’s chief executive officer, said during the company’s late-October earnings call. “But make no mistake, demand is very healthy. Even as imports have crept higher this year, domestic shipments have risen in each of the past three quarters.”

American mills have ramped up production as prices climbed and foreign supplies dwindled. US steel output rose 5.9% through the week ending Nov. 14 from a year earlier, according to the American Iron and Steel Institute. But the higher output hasn’t alleviated supply constraints, with mill outages, strong order books and declining imports limiting the amount of steel readily available to buyers.

For small manufacturers like Marlin Steel, which makes custom products from steel wire and sheet metal, that can mean a longer wait for orders.

Drew Greenblatt, CEO of Marlin Steel, says he only buys from American producers, and the orders he places with steel mills are now taking between eight and 12 weeks to fill, rather than the one- to three-day shipment time his company enjoyed a year ago. In turn, Greenblatt says his company has stocked up on inventory.

“It’s very awkward for us to have to reframe our pricing to our clients,” he said. “So I try to overbuy now so that I can keep shipping volumes to them. We’ve been buying a lot more than we really need.”

In Korea, the steel industry is dominated by giants like POSCO Holdings and Hyundai Steel Co., which have substantial capacity to produce metal and have searched for overseas markets as demand at home remains sluggish. Vietnam, meanwhile, has rapidly expanded its steelmaking capacity in recent years, supplying everything from construction steel and hot-rolled coil to pipes and galvanized sheets.

That shift has alarmed domestic producers, who have long complained about competitors from Asia that they say use the US as a dumping ground.

US steelmakers in September urged the Trump administration to investigate a surge in South Korean shipments, pointing to sharp increases in imports of construction steel, pipes and flat-rolled products. Korean steel shipments reached 519,000 tons in September alone, up 21% from August, while imports from Japan jumped 60%.

The US market is “undeniably in the midst of a significant squeeze driven by a combination of low end-customer inventory, data center demand, and seasonal restocking,” Alexander Hacking, a Citigroup analyst, wrote in a note to clients. “When this squeeze alleviates remains to be seen.”

title: Nasdaq 100 falls 2% on AI rout, tariff hike talk
article:
(Nov 25) : Wall Street’s doubts about the durability of the artificial-intelligence trade spurred selling in technology stocks, with investors also parsing talks of fresh US tariffs.

Just a day after an AI-led surge, the Nasdaq 100 sank 2%. Nvidia Corp. lost about 6%. Anthropic PBC dropped below its IPO price. While the S&P 500 edged lower, most of its firms rose. In late hours, HP Inc. and Dell Technologies Inc. gave solid outlooks.

“While we believe that the low point for stocks during this recent volatility has already been reached, we still expect continued chop as this market remains very headline-sensitive when it comes to AI,” said Rick Gardner at RGA Investments.

Fears over AI safety emerged after Axios reported that some Anthropic and OpenAI unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released.

Meantime, the US is set to announce plans to raise tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and more than a dozen other economies, according to people familiar with the matter.

However, the additional tariffs won’t lead to an overall rate that exceeds the agreed-upon levels in individual trade deals, including the pacts President Donald Trump negotiated with the EU and China, people familiar with the details said.

See also: US blacklists Megaspeed, and six firms across Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand over chip diversion risk

Investors also sifted through the latest economic data. Anxiety about inflation has yet to spoil spending appetite in the period leading up to the holiday-shopping season. US consumer confidence surged to the highest in nearly two years.

The report came on the eve of the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation metric, which is seen adding to bets that officials will raise rates in December.

Even as the Fed tightens policy, Treasuries will continue to advance over the next year, according to Joe Maher at Capital Economics.

“That’s because we think the tech-driven rout in the stock market has further to run and will prompt investors to revise down their rate expectations and trigger a ‘flight-to-safety’ into bonds,” he said.
